metadata.scope: Poore & Nemecek 2018 cradle-to-retail lifecycle emissions including land-use change and supply-chain losses (GWP100), as published by Our World in Data. Statistic: production-weighted MEANS dataset-wide; an archived MEDIAN-without-losses set exists as a documented fallback and is always disclosed when used. Weights are as-purchased raw/dry; liquids at density 1.0 so per litre = per kg (error < 1.5%). Excluded: retail-to-home transport, home cooking and refrigeration energy, household food waste. Global category means, no organic/local modifier. This boundary differs from the transport calculator's operational-only scope -- values from the two calculators must NOT be summed. Version 2 widens the dataset from 43 to 162 items. Most new items sit on a Poore & Nemecek CATEGORY row rather than a species measurement, and say so per item; a minority come from other databases at a narrower boundary and are marked as such, so they read low against the primary rows and are never compared across sources.
metadata.primary_source: Poore & Nemecek 2018 (Science 360:987-992) via Our World in Data, means with supply-chain losses
metadata.basis: kg CO2e per kg of food as-purchased (raw/dry weight); serving presets are raw/dry grams; liquids per litre = per kg at density 1.0
metadata.citation_note: CSV-row citations (OWID grapher downloads) and Poore & Nemecek accepted-manuscript figure rows are verbatim data-row transcriptions (manuscript rows with single spaces), not page sentences. CarbonCloud citations are 'product | value | value-as-of date' transcriptions: CarbonCloud live values drift over time and are corroboration-with-access-date only. The LiveLCA butter citation is a products-table row transcription (product, CO2e per kg, number of studies, single spaces), not a page sentence.
metadata.statistic_note: Three items carry statistic_sensitive: their own published mean and median differ by 2x or more (dark chocolate 2.49x, farmed fish 2.67x, tree nuts 2.15x), so which statistic the source chose dominates their value and no gap between them and another food is safe to rank. The comparison view declines to name a winner whenever one is involved. Every other pair in this dataset for which the study publishes both statistics keeps the same ordering under either one once the gap reaches 20%, which is why 20% is the threshold.

items.calculation_notes: Production-weighted global mean of Poore & Nemecek 2018's two beef rows, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Our World in Data publishes beef-herd beef (99.48) and dairy-herd beef (33.30) separately, but no label tells a shopper which herd their beef came from, so this app ships one number: 0.56 x 99.48 + 0.44 x 33.30 = 70.36. The 56/44 weights are Our World in Data's own -- around 56% of global beef production comes from dedicated beef herds and 44% from dairy herds -- and the FAO's 2013 report on greenhouse gas emissions from ruminant supply chains splits the 61.4 million tonnes of global beef the same way. Those are global production shares on a carcass-weight basis, not consumption shares, so a regional shopper sits off this mean in a known direction: European beef is majority dairy-herd (nearer 53) while US, Australian and most imported beef is majority beef-herd (nearer 86). You may see beef quoted at about 60 kg CO2e per kg elsewhere; that is Poore & Nemecek's median without supply-chain losses, whereas this dataset uses production-weighted means including losses, which run higher and better represent total global impact. Weigh the meat as bought; servings are the USDA ready-to-cook reference amount for cuts of meat, 114 g, at one, two and three portions.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for pig meat, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses -- their 'Pig Meat' row taken directly, and it already carries a processing stage of about 0.42. Bacon, cooked ham and fresh pork sausage all log here, because the only citable mass rules for them are ceilings on finished weight rather than measured yields, and each lands at or very near raw pork: US rules require cured bacon ready for slicing to weigh no more than the fresh belly it came from, and USDA processing data puts cooked ham at no more than the weight of the fresh ham, so both come out at 12.31, while fresh pork sausage may carry at most about 3% added water and no byproducts or extenders, giving about 11.94. The honest exception is jurisdiction: a UK sausage labelled 'pork' need only be 42% meat, which would give about 5.17 before the rusk, water and fat remainder, so for a legal-minimum UK sausage this figure over-states by up to about 2.4x. Two regulators resolve the same product in opposite directions and no global value exists, so the figure stays on raw pork -- it can over-state, but it never under-states. Dry-cured ham, serrano, prosciutto, salami, chorizo and pepperoni do not belong here: log those as Cured meat, which is considerably higher. Servings are USDA reference amounts: 114 g and 228 g for cuts of meat, 54 g for bacon (about three rashers), 55 g for sliced ham, and 75 g for one uncooked sausage.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Poultry Meat' group, 9.87 kg CO2e/kg, applied unchanged to turkey. It is not a measurement of turkey. Turkey is at least demonstrably inside the study: US rules count turkeys as poultry, and Poore & Nemecek's reference list includes a UK turkey-production life-cycle study (Leinonen, Williams and Kyriazakis, 2016). Nothing published separates turkey from chicken by enough to justify a different number -- the Agribalyse database puts raw turkey meat and raw chicken meat at exactly the same value (4.56), and turkey escalope and skinless chicken fillet at exactly the same value (5.58), and the SU-EATABLE LIFE database separates them by only 5-11%. Those Agribalyse figures could not be used here in any case, because a different database cannot be mixed with Poore & Nemecek's. One honest caveat that no source resolves: the poultry mean is dominated by broiler-chicken systems, and turkey grows more slowly on poorer feed conversion, so the true turkey figure is plausibly a few percent above chicken's. Weigh the meat as bought; servings are the USDA ready-to-cook reference amount for poultry cuts, 114 g, at one, two and three portions.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Poultry Meat' group, 9.87 kg CO2e/kg, applied unchanged to duck. It is not a measurement of duck. Ducks count as poultry under US rules, but unlike turkey, duck is not demonstrably inside the study: Poore & Nemecek's reference list contains no duck study at all, so this is a category number applied to a species that group does not visibly sample. There is real counter-evidence, disclosed rather than hidden: the Agribalyse database puts raw duck meat 77% above raw chicken (8.06 against 4.56), a gap wide enough that duck would deserve a figure of its own. It is still not used, for two reasons. A different database cannot be mixed with Poore & Nemecek's; and Agribalyse's own duck cuts disagree with each other by more than 3x -- magret 14.6, generic duck meat 8.06, boneless duck leg with skin 4.68 -- which reflects how emissions are divided between the products of the French mulard and foie-gras system, not biology. World duck meat is overwhelmingly Pekin duck raised in Asia. So read 4.68 to 14.6 as that Agribalyse spread across cuts of one bird, not as a range for this figure. Weigh the meat as bought; servings are the USDA ready-to-cook reference amount for poultry cuts, 114 g, at one, two and three portions.

items.calculation_notes: This is Poore & Nemecek 2018's global value for their whole 'Lamb & Mutton' group, 39.72 kg CO2e/kg, used as a small-ruminant category average and applied unchanged to goat. It is not a measurement of goat -- Poore & Nemecek's reference list contains no goat-meat study, only two dairy-goat papers. The one global model that resolves both species puts them within about 2%: the FAO's 2013 report on greenhouse gas emissions from ruminant supply chains gives sheep meat 24.0 and goat meat 23.5 kg CO2e per kg of carcass weight, so goat sits on the sheep number and a difference between goat and lamb here is not real. Counter-evidence, disclosed rather than acted on: the Agribalyse database puts raw kid goat 25% above mutton (41.3 against 33.0), but that is French milk-breed kid, a small carcass that is a by-product of dairy-goat herds rather than the meat-goat systems the FAO models globally -- and a different database cannot be mixed with Poore & Nemecek's in any case. Weigh the meat as bought; servings are the USDA ready-to-cook reference amount for cuts of meat, 114 g, at one, two and three portions.

items.calculation_notes: Derived from raw pork by the one curing loss that is published as a legal minimum. The traditional-speciality specification for Jamon Serrano, registered under EU law, requires a minimum 33% weight loss against the fresh weight of the leg, so at most 0.67 kg of finished ham comes out of each kilogram of fresh pork: 12.31 / 0.67 = 18.37, about 49% above raw pork, which is why cured meat is logged separately. No curing or smoking energy is added on top, because Poore & Nemecek's pork row already carries a processing stage and no published curing figure exists on a matching boundary -- adding one from a different boundary would double count. Read this as a floor rather than a central estimate, that is, as 'at least 18.37': the 33% is a regulatory minimum loss rather than a typical one, and it is measured on the bone-in leg, so deboning, rind and trim -- all of which raise the real ratio -- are left out. For scale, the US federal minimum for dry-cured ham is a loss of at least 18%, which would give 15.0, and the Spanish protected Jamon de Trevelez requires at least 35%, which gives 18.9. Corroboration from outside this derivation: a published life-cycle study of Parma ham on the bone reports 23.11 kg CO2e/kg on a different boundary and an Italian heavy-pig inventory, and Agribalyse's own ordering puts dry ham at about 2.07x its raw pork against the 1.49x used here, so this figure sits at the conservative end. Honest limitation: dry fermented sausages -- salami, chorizo, pepperoni -- log here too, yet no published weight yield exists for them anywhere, since the US rules that would set one are reserved and blank and the Spanish protected specifications for Salchichon de Vic and Chorizo de Cantimpalos fix diameter, curing days, fat, protein and sugars but no weight loss. They ride this figure rather than pork because they lose 25-45% of their water, and pork would put them well too low. Servings come from the USDA reference amount for dried meats, 30 g, whose own row text names Parma ham and pepperoni, at one, two and three amounts.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for milk, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Milk is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry. Yogurt carries this exact same figure: under the US standards of identity yogurt is made from milk one to one by mass -- fermentation converts lactose to lactic acid inside the same mass and nothing is removed -- so milk and yogurt are one number with two names here, and a difference between them is not real. Flavoured milk and milkshakes log here too: a retail milkshake declares about 88% milk plus roughly 7% added sugar, which works out within about 5% of plain milk, and its unquantified extras (buttermilk powder, cocoa) push back towards plain milk rather than away. The 240 ml glass is the FDA reference amount for milk at density 1.0 and the 330 ml bottle is a retail milkshake size that serves the flavoured-milk entries; the 200 ml glass is carried over from an earlier version and has no independent source.

items.calculation_notes: This is derived from milk rather than measured. Under the US standards of identity, milk must be at least 3.25% milkfat and 8.25% milk solids not fat, and yogurt must meet the same minimums using cream, milk, partially skimmed milk or skim milk as its dairy inputs -- fermentation converts lactose to lactic acid inside the same mass and nothing is removed -- so yogurt is one to one with milk by mass and carries Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for milk unchanged, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Milk and yogurt therefore share this one number, and a difference between them here is not real. The honest reason it is derived instead of taken from a published yogurt study is that every published yogurt footprint comes out below the milk it is made from -- Agribalyse puts plain yogurt at 1.89, about 0.6x the milk figure -- which cannot be right for a product that removes nothing. Set yogurts fortified with milk powder run slightly above one to one and this takes no credit for that. The 170 g pot is the FDA reference amount for yogurt and the 125 g pot is a standard European retail pot; the 400 g family tub is recorded as a Japanese pack size but has no cited basis behind it.

items.calculation_notes: This is a constructed multiplier, not a life-cycle study of Greek yogurt. Karastamatis and colleagues (2022, Foods) measured the straining step directly: 100 g of set yogurt gives about 30.5 g of strained yogurt once the acid whey is drained, so about 3.28 kg of yogurt goes into 1 kg of the finished product, and because yogurt is one to one with milk by mass that is also about 3.28 kg of milk per kg. Applied to Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for milk, that gives 10.33. Straining for 24 hours instead of immediately raises the yield to 33 g per 100 g in the same study, which would give about 9.55; the figure here uses immediate straining, which is both industry-typical and the more conservative of the two. No credit is taken for the drained acid whey -- it is treated as waste. Skyr and labneh log here as well: they are strained at broadly similar ratios, but no yield was sourced for them specifically. No database resolves strained yogurt on its own -- Agribalyse returns the same value as plain yogurt -- which is why the measured yield was used instead. The 170 g pot is the FDA reference amount for yogurt, 200 g is a USDA container portion and 150 g a retail pot.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for cheese, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. It is a single, undifferentiated cheese entry: the study does not separate cheddar from mozzarella from feta, so we make no claim about which variety is better. Working a specific variety back out of milk does not help either -- the milk-to-cheese yield implied by this figure is about 7.6 kg of milk per kg of cheese, below every published cheddar yield, so the arithmetic inverts against the source. Cottage cheese and ricotta sit on this same row and carry the same number, and milk powder lands slightly above it, so neither of those gaps should be read as a ranking. The 30 g portion is the FDA reference amount for cheese and the 5 g measure is its reference amount for grated hard cheese, which covers the grated entries; the 22 g slice is carried over from an earlier version and has no independent source.

It is not a measurement of cottage cheese or ricotta: the study publishes no detail below the cheese category, so the category average is the only honest figure available. Cottage cheese does belong to the category -- the US standard of identity defines it as a soft uncured cheese made by mixing dry curd with a creaming mixture, at least 4% milkfat and no more than 80% moisture, and files it among cheeses and related cheese products. The direction of the error is disclosed rather than quietly patched: the cheese average is dominated by ripened, low-moisture cheeses, while cottage cheese is up to 80% water and is curded from largely de-fatted milk with the cream leaving as a co-product, so this figure very likely overstates it. It is not corrected because correcting it would need a milk-to-cheese yield, and that yield comes out inverted against the source. The 110 g serving is the FDA reference amount for cottage cheese; 225 g and 113 g are USDA portion weights (one cup of small curd, and 4 oz).

items.calculation_notes: Read this one as "at least" -- it is a documented floor, not an average. It is built from the US legal minimum composition for ice cream, which must contain at least 10% milkfat and 10% nonfat milk solids (20% total milk solids) and must weigh at least 4.5 pounds to the gallon. Commercial whole milk carries about 11.9% total solids, so 20% milk solids works out at about 1.68 kg of milk per kg of ice cream, which against Poore & Nemecek 2018's milk mean is about 5.29. The same minimum weight implies at least about 35.6% total food solids, leaving about 15.6% that is not milk solids and is essentially all sweetener; against their cane sugar mean that adds about 0.50, for 5.78 in total. It is a floor in several ways: it uses the legal minimum milk-solids content and takes no credit for egg solids (allowed up to 1.4%), stabilisers, inclusions or the cream co-product route, and real ice cream -- premium especially -- carries more milk solids than the minimum; using the regulation's minimum milk composition instead of commercial averages would put it about 3% higher, near 5.98. One caveat matters more than the arithmetic: a 500 ml tub is not 500 g, because ice cream is aerated. Legal-minimum ice cream weighs about 539 g per litre, so 500 ml of it can be as little as 270 g, and a typical tub measured from USDA portion data comes out around 279 g for 500 ml. That is why every serving here is in grams and why the tub preset is labelled 279 g rather than 500: 88 g is the FDA reference amount (two thirds of a cup) converted at that density and 66 g is the USDA half-cup portion.

items.calculation_notes: This is whole milk powder, worked out as milk with the water taken out. USDA composition tables put dry whole milk at 97.5% total solids against whole milk's 11.9%, so about 8.18 kg of milk goes into 1 kg of powder, and against Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for milk that gives 25.77. Two independent cross-checks agree within a few percent, which is what pure water removal should do: milkfat alone gives 8.03 and milk solids not fat alone 8.24. USDA's own farm-milk-equivalent factors for dry whole milk -- 7.36 on a milkfat basis and 8.26 on a skim-solids basis -- bracket it, giving a range of roughly 23.18 to 26.02. This lands slightly above the cheese figure, by about 8%, because powder retains essentially all of the milk solids; that small gap should not be read as milk powder being worse than cheese. Scope caveat: this is whole milk powder. Skimmed milk powder is a different product, concentrated further on a skim-solids basis with the cream leaving as an uncredited co-product, so logging it here would understate it. Powder is hard to judge against a milk intuition, so the measures here are fixed: 29 g is the powder for one 240 ml glass at this item's own concentration factor, and 32 g and 128 g are the USDA quarter-cup and cup portions.

items.calculation_notes: Margarine has no life-cycle measurement of its own, so this is derived from the vegetable oil (sunflower / rapeseed) figure using the US standard of identity, which requires margarine to contain not less than 80% fat: 0.80 x 4.02 = 3.21. That makes it a floor rather than a central estimate -- it counts only the fat, and nothing for the water, salt, emulsifiers, added vitamin A or packaging that make up the rest of the tub, even though the figure is applied to the whole as-bought weight. The 80% is a real composition and not just a legal minimum: USDA data for stick and tub margarine measures 80.2 to 80.7 g of fat per 100 g, and the Japanese (MEXT) composition tables put margarine at 83 to 84 g while listing fat spread separately at 69 g, drawing the line in the same place the US rule does. The assumption behind the number is that the fat is rapeseed or sunflower oil. The regulation permits any vegetable or rendered animal fat, so the answer forks by recipe: a palm-blend margarine works out at 0.80 x 7.50 = about 6.0, roughly 1.9x higher, and many European tub margarines declare rapeseed and palm together in unstated proportions. The seed-oil line is the one shown here and the two forks are not averaged. The underlying oil figure is a Poore & Nemecek 2018 global mean from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses, converted from their per-litre basis to a weight (see the vegetable oil entry). Margarine, mayonnaise and ketchup all land close together, between about 3.1 and 3.5, and because each is built up from its declared recipe rather than measured, the ordering between them is not meaningful; margarine is also not independent of the vegetable oil figure it comes from. The presets are the weight of the product as bought.

items.calculation_notes: This is Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for peas, including land-use change and supply-chain losses, used as the pulse figure for a podded legume seed eaten as a protein food -- it is not a measurement of edamame. No life-cycle study of edamame exists and Agribalyse has no edamame entry, so there is nothing closer to use, and the frozen supply chain most edamame travels through is not in this number either. It is deliberately not placed on the tofu figure: tofu carries roughly 0.79 kg CO2e/kg of processing on its own, while edamame is an unprocessed fresh or frozen vegetable at about 72% water, so a tofu anchor would overstate it by around 3x. The basis is shelled beans, the edible part: Japan's MEXT food composition table gives a 45% refuse rate for raw edamame, so pods weigh about 1.8x the beans inside them and about 145 g of pods gives 80 g of beans -- if you are weighing pods, enter about 55% of that weight. USDA's edamame records show no refuse at all because they are already shelled, which is why the pod fraction comes from the Japanese table. For a sense of scale from a different source group, Agribalyse puts whole soybean grain at 1.25, fresh broad beans to shell at 0.858 and raw green beans at 0.447.

items.calculation_notes: This is the general tinned-pulse figure rather than a measurement of chickpeas: it is the same number the tinned-bean entry carries, because rebuilding that entry's recipe with chickpea composition instead lands within 4% of it. The basis is drained weight -- weigh the chickpeas after tipping the tin into a sieve, not the whole contents of the tin (a 400 g tin drains to about 240 g). The build behind it is Poore & Nemecek 2018's global average for other pulses, 1.79, spread over the water the pulses take up in the tin, plus a term for the canning step and the steel can, which comes to about 1.64 on chickpea composition against 1.71 on bean composition -- close enough that the two share one number rather than being split apart. The hydration comes from USDA composition data: chickpeas are 7.7% water dry against about 67 to 69% water once canned and drained, roughly 2.9x, trimmed slightly for caution exactly as in the beans build. One source disagrees and is not used: Agribalyse puts tinned drained chickpeas 52% above tinned drained kidney beans, yet the same database puts the dry forms within 5% of each other, and its tinned chickpea entry carries poor data quality -- a 5% gap in the raw ingredient cannot become a 52% gap after canning, so we treat that as an artefact. The canning and can term comes from a CarbonCloud model of tinned beans and stands as corroboration, not as an independent measurement of chickpeas.

items.calculation_notes: The basis here is the whole contents of the tin, sauce included -- unlike the tinned pulses next to it, which are drained -- so enter what goes on the plate, sauce and all: half a 415 g tin is about 207.5 g. No life-cycle study of baked beans is used. The figure is built up from Heinz's own declared ingredient percentages for beans in tomato sauce (beans 51%, tomatoes 34%). Under EU and UK labelling rules those percentages are the weight at the time the ingredient is used, and ingredients used concentrated or dried may be declared before rehydration, so 'beans 51%' is soaked bean weight rather than dry beans; the declared protein confirms it, because 51% dry navy beans would give about 11.4 g protein per 100 g while the label works out to 4.8 g. Solving from the protein instead gives about 0.204 kg of dry beans per kg of tin, an implied hydration of 2.5x -- the same figure the tinned beans entry uses. The build per kg of tin contents is then dry beans on Poore & Nemecek's other-pulses average, tomatoes on their fresh tomato average, about 3% added sugar on their beet sugar figure and 1% modified cornflour on their maize figure, giving about 1.15 for the ingredients, plus 0.67 for the canning step and the can, for a total of 1.82. Finished-goods transport is not added on top, because those ingredient figures already run from farm to retail. The total is deliberately conservative on the high side: the tomato term alone is 39% of it and uses a global fresh-tomato average inflated by heated-greenhouse growers, whereas bean sauce is made from field-grown processing tomatoes -- at half the tomato figure the total falls to 1.46, the bottom of the disclosed range. USDA's own composition for tinned baked beans supports the recipe, at 4.75 g protein per 100 g against Heinz's 4.8. Agribalyse's beans-in-tomato-sauce entry is no use as a cross-check, because its ingredient breakdown contains no tomato at all.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for shelled tree nuts, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Their functional unit is 1 kg of shell-free, dry nut, so weigh in-shell nuts after shelling -- a bag of in-shell pistachios is only about half kernel by weight. This figure includes a large land-use-change carbon credit (-3.26) for orchards planted on former cropland, and that credit is doing all the work: without it the same stages total about 3.69, roughly 8.5x higher, which would place tree nuts about 14% above peanuts (3.23) instead of far below. Treat the gap between the two as an accounting choice, not a measured difference, and for the same reason do not read this number as making nuts the lowest-impact protein there is. Almond, cashew, walnut, hazelnut and pistachio all share this one number -- the two databases that separate them rank them in close to opposite order, so we do not claim one is better than another. Peanuts are a legume with their own, much higher figure: log them as Peanuts, and log a mixed bag of nuts containing peanuts there too. Chestnuts are not covered, because they are eaten fresh at roughly half water and a dry-kernel factor is the wrong basis for them.

items.calculation_notes: Derived from the peanut figure rather than measured on its own. The US standard of identity requires peanut butter to be ground roasted peanuts with seasoning and stabilisers together capped at 10% of the finished weight, so it is at least 90% peanuts by law, and the all-peanut jars on the shelf are what is modelled. A roasting weight loss is then applied from USDA composition data: raw peanuts are 6.5% water and dry-roasted peanuts 1.81%, a roast yield of about 0.952, so about 1.05 kg of raw peanuts per kg of butter, giving 3.23 x 1.05 = 3.39. That last step is contested and you should know it: Poore & Nemecek's peanut row is already defined on roasted, shell-free nuts, so the roasting loss is arguably being counted twice and peanut butter may really sit at essentially the plain peanut figure of 3.23 -- either way the two are within a few percent of each other. Grinding energy and the glass jar are not included, so in that respect the number is conservative on the low side, and even at the legal minimum of 90% peanuts plus 10% added oil the total stays above the plain peanut figure. Agribalyse supports the ordering from a separate database: its peanut butter (4.06) sits at about 0.97x its own peanuts (4.18), essentially level with them rather than anywhere near half. A published SU-EATABLE LIFE figure of 1.84 is 43% below the peanut value it is built from, which is not physically possible, and is not used. Weigh what comes out of the jar. Peanut spread by origin is large and unresolved inside the one global peanut row, so no per-origin claims.

items.calculation_notes: This number comes from Agribalyse, the French national food life-cycle database, and not from Poore & Nemecek: it is Agribalyse's sunflower seed entry, 2.91. Agribalyse draws its boundary from field to plate, so it includes the consumption stage, and it counts direct land-use change only -- that is not the same accounting as the Poore & Nemecek items elsewhere in the app, so a number from a different database should not be read against them, and any gap you see between them is mostly method rather than food. Pumpkin seeds are logged here too rather than separately: Agribalyse's cucurbit-seed entry is 3.49, about 20% higher, but it carries the worst data-quality rating in that database, so the sunflower value is the one used and 3.49 is disclosed as the top of the range. The measurement itself is of sunflower seed. These seeds are deliberately not placed on Poore & Nemecek's tree-nut figure, because that figure nets a large land-use-change credit for orchards planted on former cropland, and sunflower and pumpkin are annual field crops with no orchard to credit. As a direction check, this reads about 10% below Poore & Nemecek's peanuts and about 30% below Agribalyse's own peanuts -- the gap narrows across the two databases but does not flip. Basis is as-purchased kernels, and Agribalyse's roasted, salted sunflower entry is also 2.91, so roasting does not change the number.

items.calculation_notes: Derived, not measured: Poore & Nemecek publish no flour row. Their 'Wheat & Rye' figure of 1.57 is per kilogram of bread, and bread is around 39% water while flour is only about 14%, so the same weight of flour carries roughly 1.4x as much wheat dry matter and cannot simply take the bread number. Re-basing gives about 2.58 kg CO2e per kilogram of wheat dry matter, and flour is 86% dry matter, which is the 2.22 shown here. This is a water correction and nothing else: it assumes a kilogram of wheat dry matter carries the same emissions in flour as in bread, so no milling step is added and no baking energy is taken back out, and your own baking is not counted at all. The weakest link is that Poore & Nemecek never say how wet their bread is -- the 39% comes from a Japanese composition table for sliced bread, and if their loaf is drier, say 35% water, this and every other wheat-derived figure falls by about 6%. Agribalyse independently places wheat flour slightly above its own baguette, the same direction this method predicts. Weigh flour dry, before anything is added to it.

items.calculation_notes: Derived, not measured: Poore & Nemecek publish no pasta row. Their 'Wheat & Rye' figure of 1.57 is per kilogram of bread, which is around 39% water, while dry pasta is only about 11% water -- a kilogram of dry pasta therefore holds roughly 46% more wheat dry matter than a kilogram of bread, and taking the bread number directly would undercount it by that much. Re-basing the anchor gives about 2.58 kg CO2e per kilogram of wheat dry matter, and dry pasta is 89% dry matter, which is 2.29. This is a water correction only, so the difference between baking a loaf and drying pasta is not counted, and neither is boiling it in your kitchen. A second, equally citable route exists: Poore & Nemecek also publish a calorie basis for the same row, and bridging on calories instead of water gives 2.02, about 12% lower, because their bread is more energy-dense than the sliced bread the moisture figure comes from and may simply be drier. The two routes bracket the answer between 2.02 and 2.29, and the figure shown is the higher, less flattering end. Weigh pasta dry: 55 g uncooked becomes about 120 g cooked, a little over 2x, so enter the dry weight. Pasta sitting above bread is not evidence that pasta is worse -- bread is the measured product, pasta is worked back from it, and what separates them is water.

items.calculation_notes: Derived, not measured: Poore & Nemecek publish no noodle row, so this comes from their bread figure of 1.57, re-based for water. Fresh noodles are about 33% water against bread's 39%, which gives about 2.58 kg CO2e per kilogram of wheat dry matter and 1.73 for the noodles. Udon, ramen and soba all share this one number: Japan's national composition tables put fresh udon, fresh ramen, fresh soba and Okinawa soba between 32.3% and 33.5% water, a spread of about 1%, so a difference between them here is not real. Soba is the one genuine unknown -- Japan's fair-competition code for fresh noodles sets its legal minimum at 30% buckwheat flour and no more than 70% wheat, but Poore & Nemecek have no buckwheat figure, so buckwheat is carried at the wheat rate; even the most generous defensible uplift, borrowed from Agribalyse's own buckwheat-to-wheat flour ratio, would raise soba only about 14%, while a true 100% buckwheat soba would be around 48% higher. The basis is the raw fresh noodle, so weigh it before boiling; the boiling itself is not counted. Pre-boiled packs, the kind sold ready to rinse, are already converted back to a fresh-equivalent weight in the presets -- a 210 g udon pack counts as about 79 g of fresh noodle and a 180 g soba pack as about 86 g -- because boiling roughly doubles to trebles the weight. And because Poore & Nemecek never state their bread's moisture, the whole figure moves about 6% either way with that assumption.

items.calculation_notes: Derived, not measured, and it covers the noodle block only -- the seasoning sachet is not included. Two things are added together: the wheat dough, and the palm oil the noodles absorb when they are flash-fried at the factory, which is counted here rather than ignored. Japan's national composition tables list fried and non-fried instant noodles side by side with seasoning excluded, and the fat difference between them, 19.6 g against 1.9 g per 100 g, gives about 17.7 g of absorbed frying oil per 100 g of noodles; the fatty-acid profile of the fried row is textbook palm oil, so palm is what gets priced. Per kilogram of noodle block that is about 786 g of wheat dry matter at 2.58 kg CO2e per kg, which is 2.03, plus 177 g of palm oil at 7.32 per kg, which is 1.30 -- 3.32 in total, or roughly 1.45x the same weight of dry pasta. Nothing is added on top for the factory's own energy, so read 3.32 as a floor rather than a central estimate, and boiling the noodles at home is not counted either. One known soft spot: Poore & Nemecek measure palm oil per litre rather than per kilogram, and correcting for palm oil's real density would push this item to 3.45, about 4% higher. The one ready-made database figure for instant noodles reads below that same database's dry pasta, which cannot be right for a noodle carrying almost a fifth of its weight in added oil, so it is not used here. Instant noodles are logged by the block rather than by weight because they are sold that way -- a standard cup-noodle block is 65 g.

items.calculation_notes: Direct global mean for potatoes, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses -- the lowest-impact staple here, with a farm stage of 0.19 and almost no land-use change. Their unit is 1 kg of soil-free tuber, so weigh whole raw potatoes, soil off and skin on. Crisps and fries are processed products and belong on the treats row instead: 'chips' means fries in American English and crisps in British English, so log them by what they actually are.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for tomatoes, Poore & Nemecek 2018, farm to retail and including land-use change and supply-chain losses. This is a real single-crop figure rather than a group average, but the mean hides one of the widest spreads in the dataset: 90% of the study's tomatoes fall between 0.37 and 12.62 kg CO2e per kg, the raw observations run from about 0.2 to 29, the median tomato is only 0.65, and roughly 80% of the total impact comes from a quarter of the producers. That is the heated greenhouse at work -- a Dutch winter tomato and a Spanish field tomato are the same crop two orders of magnitude apart. Since the median tomato at 0.65 is barely above Poore & Nemecek's general vegetable average of 0.53, 2.09 is the honest mean but a poor basis for saying tomatoes are worse than other vegetables; how and where they were grown is what actually moves the number. Basis is as-purchased fresh weight, not edible weight. Tinned, chopped and sieved tomatoes log here too: weight for weight an as-sold peeled or chopped pack is about the same as fresh, because the Codex standard for preserved tomatoes allows only tomato-derived packing liquid, and passata is included as well since no citable concentration ratio places it between 1.0x and about 1.56x fresh. A medium tomato is 123 g and the standard US serving 85 g; the 400 g tin is a retail pack size rather than a measured one.

items.calculation_notes: Derived from Poore & Nemecek 2018's tomato figure by a concentration ratio, so it is per kg of paste, not per kg of the tomatoes that went into it. The Codex standard for processed tomato concentrates sets paste at no less than 24% natural soluble solids and fixes 4.5% as the reference value for fresh tomato precisely so a concentrate can be worked back to its fresh input: that is about 5.3 kg of fresh tomatoes per kg of paste, and 2.09 x 5.33 gives 11.14. Read it as a floor rather than a central estimate -- driving roughly 4.3 kg of water out of every kilogram of paste is not free, but no citable figure for evaporator energy exists, so none has been added. 24% is also the bottom of the grade: double-concentrated pastes at 28-30% soluble solids would be roughly 1.2x this number, and a soluble-solids ratio is not the same as a total-solids ratio. Basis is salt-free paste as sold, weighed as bought. Watch the naming, because the two conventions differ by roughly 3x: a UK tube of 'tomato puree' is Codex paste at 24% solids or more and belongs here, while US 'tomato puree' is the much weaker 8-24% grade. Codex itself defines only two concentrate grades, 7% and 24%; the 8% puree grade is a US regulation, not a Codex one.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Brassicas' group, not a measurement of cabbage, and it includes land-use change and supply-chain losses. The group is built around head cabbage -- white, red and savoy, all Brassica oleracea -- while napa cabbage has its own entry because it is a different species. Poore & Nemecek never publish which species sit inside their produce groups (the only vegetables they confirm sampling are tomatoes, lettuce, cucumber, green beans and green peas), so membership here follows FAO's commodity definitions, which file every brassica in the app into just two Brassica oleracea commodities. Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, napa cabbage, pak choi and Brussels sprouts all share this one number, so a difference between them here would not be real -- and Poore & Nemecek's four vegetable group averages of 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 sit on such heavily overlapping distributions that ranking one vegetable against another is not meaningful either. The group mean of 0.51 sits well above its own median of 0.35, with most farms between 0.23 and 0.97 across 32 observations from 40 farms, all on an as-purchased fresh-weight basis rather than edible weight -- so weigh the cabbage as bought, outer leaves and all.

The group mean of 0.43 sits against a median of 0.40, with most farms between 0.24 and 0.56 across 30 observations from 43 farms -- one of the thinnest groups in the study. items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Vegetables' group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of spinach, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Spinach is unambiguously a vegetable and has its own FAO commodity, so the catch-all is not a misclassification: it is simply the only row Poore & Nemecek publishes that spinach can go on, and the study never says which species are inside that row. Chard logs here on the same basis, since the FAO's residual fresh-vegetables commodity names beets and chards explicitly; shungiku, the chrysanthemum green, is routed here by inference because the FAO does not name it anywhere. Japanese composition tables put chard at no waste at all and shungiku at about 1% once the base is trimmed, rising to 15% if you buy it with the roots still on. The basis is 1 kg of fresh vegetable as purchased rather than edible weight, so weigh the bunch or the bag as bought, before any trimming. The catch-all hides a very wide range: 66 farm observations spanning roughly 0.09 to 12 kg CO2e per kg, with a median of 0.42 against the 0.53 mean and most between about 0.23 and 0.97. Poore & Nemecek's four vegetable groups land at 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 on overlapping data, so a gap between two vegetables here is not a real difference.

Green beans are one of only five vegetables the study confirms it sampled, alongside tomatoes, lettuce, cucumber and green peas; beyond those five it never publishes what is inside its produce groups. The FAO splits them into two crops -- green beans for shelling and string beans not for shelling -- and both log here. There is a real basis mismatch worth knowing about: the production statistics underneath figures like this one count green beans and green peas with their pods on, and pods are 40 to 50% of the weight for peas and up to 70% for broad beans, while what you buy and weigh is the trimmed retail product. No source splits the study's observations into podded and shelled, so no correction has been made and the figure is left as published. The basis is otherwise 1 kg of fresh vegetable as purchased, not edible weight, so weigh the beans as bought. The catch-all hides a very wide range: 66 farm observations from roughly 0.09 to 12 kg CO2e per kg, a median of 0.42 against the 0.53 mean, and most between about 0.23 and 0.97. Poore & Nemecek's four vegetable groups land at 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 on overlapping data, so a gap between two vegetables here is not real.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Vegetables' group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of bean sprouts. Sprouts fit that group worse than almost anything else placed on it: they are grown indoors on water in trays over about five days, with no field, no fertiliser, no land-use change and effectively no losses in transport or ripening, so they have almost nothing in common with the field crops that fill the row, and no observation in the study is known to cover them. FAO's residual fresh-vegetable commodity does at least name soybean sprouts explicitly. The error runs the safe way -- 0.53 almost certainly overstates sprouts rather than flattering them -- and moyashi is one of the most-eaten vegetables in Japan, so it is included with this label rather than left out. Poore & Nemecek never publish which species sit inside their produce groups: the only vegetables they confirm sampling are tomatoes, lettuce, cucumber, green beans and green peas. Their functional unit is 1 kg of fresh vegetable, so weigh the bag as bought rather than after trimming. The group hides a wide spread: the middle observation is 0.42 against this mean of 0.53, the 10th-to-90th range is 0.23 to 0.97, and the 66 underlying farm observations span more than a hundredfold. Their four vegetable averages sit at 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 on overlapping distributions, so a difference between two vegetables here is not a real difference. One note on portions: the US regulatory reference amount for sprouts is a volume (a quarter cup), not a weight, and the 26 g option is that volume converted using the USDA 104 g cup, so the 104 g portion is the better default.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Vegetables' group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of peas. It covers the garden pea you buy fresh or frozen. Green peas are in fact one of only five vegetables the study confirms it sampled, but a group average still cannot resolve one vegetable from another, so mangetout, sugar snaps and petits pois all share this number and a difference between them here is not real. Dry split peas are a different food: the study's separate 'Peas' row, at 0.98, is defined as 1 kg of dry pea without pod at a pulse-like protein density, so split peas, marrowfat and guisantes secos are not covered by this item, and the widely repeated line that peas emit about 1 kg per kg belongs to that dry row, not to a bag of frozen peas -- using it here would overstate them by about 85% and put them above the green beans on the next shelf. FAO likewise treat green peas and dry peas as separate commodities. There is one honest open question about the basis: FAO warn that national production figures for green peas usually include the pods, which are 40-50% of the weight, while a frozen bag is already shelled, and no source splits the study's vegetable observations into podded and shelled -- so no correction is applied, but on a fully shelled basis the figure could be as high as 1.06, twice this value. The study's functional unit is 1 kg of fresh vegetable, so weigh what you buy. Inside the group the middle observation is 0.42 against this mean of 0.53, the 10th-to-90th range is 0.23 to 0.97, and the underlying farm observations span more than a hundredfold; the study's four vegetable averages sit at 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 on overlapping distributions, so vegetable-against-vegetable rankings are not defensible.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Vegetables' group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of bamboo shoots. Bamboo shoots at least clearly belong in that group: they are the first named entry in FAO's residual fresh-vegetable commodity. Two caveats follow, neither of them fatal. FAO describe vegetables as mainly annual plants, whereas bamboo is a perennial grove cut from an established stand with no yearly ploughing, planting or establishment cost, so 0.53 probably overstates takenoko -- the safe direction. The basis matters more here than for almost any other vegetable: a raw shoot is 50% waste in the Japanese composition tables (60% for small varieties such as hachiku and madake) and 71% in the USDA table, so weighing the peeled, trimmed shoot against this as-bought figure leaves you 2 to 3.5 times low -- weigh the shoot whole, as purchased. Most bamboo shoots are sold already boiled and vacuum-packed rather than raw, and that is a drained, cooked product on a different basis from this raw one: the 131 g tin option is a drained weight, and no separate boiled figure is offered because there is no citable ratio for boiling loss or drained yield. Poore & Nemecek never publish which species sit inside their produce groups; the only vegetables they confirm sampling are tomatoes, lettuce, cucumber, green beans and green peas. The group also hides a wide spread -- middle observation 0.42 against this mean of 0.53, a 10th-to-90th range of 0.23 to 0.97, and 66 farm observations spanning more than a hundredfold -- and their four vegetable averages sit at 0.43, 0.50, 0.51 and 0.53 on overlapping distributions, so a difference between two vegetables here is not real.

items.calculation_notes: Mushrooms are one of the few vegetables here that do not come from Poore & Nemecek. The figure is from Robinson and colleagues' 2018 life-cycle assessment of Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom) production in the USA: a production-weighted average across 22 growing facilities, on a 100-year global warming basis without carbon-climate feedback. The often-quoted range of 2.13 to 2.95 from that paper's abstract is not a spread across farms -- it is the span across different time horizons and feedback assumptions -- and this dataset uses the 100-year figure throughout, which is 2.13. A mushroom is not a field crop: it is grown indoors on a composted straw and manure substrate that is itself manufactured over weeks, in rooms held at temperature and humidity, and the compost and the climate control are the footprint. That is why the catch-all vegetable average of 0.53 would be about 4 times too low here and would suggest mushrooms cost about the same as lettuce. The real spread across the literature is wide: published values run from about 0.52 to 4.41 kg CO2e per kg, roughly eightfold, driven by the electricity and fuel mix behind composting and climate control rather than by anything agronomic. Because this comes from a different study on a narrower boundary -- cradle to facility gate, 1 kg of fresh product at 92% moisture, with facility construction excluded, against Poore & Nemecek's farm-to-retail figures including supply-chain losses -- a number from it should not be read against the Poore & Nemecek items as a ranking; the narrower boundary if anything widens the gap rather than explaining it. Species caveat: the measurement is of button mushrooms on composted substrate, while shiitake, enoki, shimeji, maitake and eryngii are different species grown on sterilised sawdust in bags or bottles, and enoki and shimeji have never been measured at all. Shiitake sits here because the one shiitake-specific published value, 1.87, is within about 12% of 2.13. CarbonCloud publishes 0.26 for fresh button mushrooms, but that page carries no version or date and sits 2 to 8 times below every peer-reviewed value, so it is not used, and Agribalyse has no raw button-mushroom entry. Weigh mushrooms as bought; the 250 g punnet option is a retail pack size rather than a sourced portion weight.

items.calculation_notes: This is a single modelled value from Agribalyse, the French government's food life-cycle database -- its row for raw green asparagus, version 3.2 -- and not a measured average across farms: the database publishes one number per product with no distribution behind it. It runs all the way from the farm to the consumer, cooking at home included, and counts only direct land-use change, so it stands on different footing from the Poore & Nemecek figures used for most vegetables and should not be read against them as a ranking. The modelled breakdown is roughly 0.97 at the farm, 0.42 in transport and 0.22 in the home. Transport is the important caveat: Agribalyse's own air-freight marker for this product is set to no, so 1.64 describes sea- and road-freighted asparagus only, there is no air-freighted entry, and this is not an average across transport modes -- it does not cover flown asparagus. Schwarz and colleagues (2016) put transport alone for Peruvian air-freighted asparagus at 11.12 kg CO2e per kg, against 0.03 for Belgian asparagus trucked within Belgium; that transport component on its own is more than six times this entire farm-to-consumer figure, and it is the top of the range quoted here even though it is a transport component rather than a full life-cycle result. Stoessel and colleagues (2012) find the same shape -- a 16- to 19-fold range from locally grown to air-freighted -- but publish no per-kilogram asparagus number, so the widely circulated 12.2 figure attributed to them is not theirs. Green asparagus is the variant most likely to have flown, because losses make it unsuitable for sea freight from overseas. Weigh spears as bought. A newer Agribalyse release gives 1.21 for the same product but reports the same data-quality score for every product in the file, which reads as a placeholder, so the version 3.2 value is kept.

items.calculation_notes: Dried shiitake takes the fresh mushroom figure -- 2.13 kg CO2e per kg, from Robinson and colleagues' 2018 assessment of US button-mushroom production -- and applies the concentration that drying causes. Fresh shiitake is 89.6% water and dried shiitake 9.1%, so dry matter goes from about 10% to about 91% of the weight, a factor of about 8.7, giving roughly 18.6 kg CO2e per kg of dried mushrooms. Both Japanese composition entries carry the same 20% stem waste, so that part cancels out. The basis is dry weight: weigh the mushrooms dry, before soaking, because soaking multiplies the weight without changing the emissions. What this number does not include is any drying energy at all -- it is purely the moisture concentration, so read it as 'at least': sun-dried shiitake would sit close to it, and commercial hot-air-dried shiitake above it by an unknown amount. It also carries over the caveats of the fresh figure it is built on, which measures button mushrooms grown on composted substrate in US facilities -- a different species, and a different study from the Poore & Nemecek vegetables, so it should not be ranked against them. The point of having the row at all is that 5 g of dried shiitake is not free.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Fruit' group -- a catch-all row that collects the fruits the study did not measure separately -- not a measurement of melon. It is their mean including land-use change and supply-chain losses, and their functional unit is 1 kg of fresh fruit as bought, so weigh the melon whole and uncut. Melon is an awkward fit here, because FAO does not treat it as a fruit at all: melons and cantaloupes get vegetable codes on the grounds that, unlike orchard fruit, they are temporary crops. If the study followed those groupings, melon would belong on the 'Other Vegetables' average of 0.53 instead of 1.05 -- a factor of 2 -- and the study never says which way it went, which is why the range on this item runs 0.53 to 1.05; we use the higher of the two rather than the flattering one. Almost half a melon by weight is rind, seed cavity and cutting loss (USDA puts refuse at 49%), so a cubed-flesh weight entered against this whole-fruit figure comes out roughly 2x low. The group behind the number is very uneven: its median is 0.72 against a mean of 1.05, most of the farms in it fall between 0.35 and 2.93, and a quarter of the growers account for 57% of the emissions -- the second most skewed plant group in the study, after tomatoes. The study also never publishes which species sit in each of its produce groups, so a melon-versus-another-fruit comparison built on this figure is not meaningful. We list melon with the fruit because that is where people look for it.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole 'Other Fruit' group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of watermelon. It includes land-use change and supply-chain losses, on a unit of 1 kg of fresh fruit as bought, so weigh the melon whole rather than the flesh. As with melon, the grouping is genuinely ambiguous: FAO files watermelon (Citrullus vulgaris) with the vegetables because it is a temporary crop rather than an orchard crop, so the honest figure sits somewhere between the 'Other Vegetables' average of 0.53 and the 'Other Fruit' average of 1.05 -- a factor of 2, and the study does not say which grouping it used. That is what the 0.53 to 1.05 range on this item means, and we use the higher, less flattering end. Rind, seeds and cutting loss come to 48% of the fruit by USDA's reckoning, so diced flesh weighed against this figure reads about 1.9x low. The default 280 g serving is FDA's, watermelon being one of only two fruits it carves out of the generic 140 g fruit portion. The group itself is skewed -- median 0.72 against a mean of 1.05, and a quarter of its growers behind 57% of its emissions -- and the study never lists the species in each group, so small differences between fruits here are not real differences.

servings.name_en: Half an avocado, flesh only (75 g)
servings.name_ja: アボカド半分・果肉のみ（75g）

items.calculation_notes: This figure comes from Agribalyse, the French environmental agency ADEME's food database, and is its value for raw avocado pulp. The basis is edible flesh with the stone and skin already removed, so every portion here is flesh only -- weigh what you actually eat. Logging a whole 201 g avocado against this number would overstate it by about 1.35x, since a quarter or so of the fruit is stone and skin (USDA puts refuse at 26%, Japan's MEXT at 30%; we use USDA because the portions are built from USDA data). Agribalyse measures to the consumer and counts only direct land-use change, so it is built differently from Poore & Nemecek 2018: a number from this database should not be lined up against the Poore & Nemecek fruit and vegetable figures elsewhere in the app, in either direction. As a sanity check rather than a second value, a 2024 peer-reviewed study of South African avocados shipped to Europe by refrigerated sea freight reports 0.905 kg CO2e per kg of whole fruit before offsets; putting this figure on the same whole-fruit basis gives about 1.15, the same magnitude and ordering, which is where the 0.905 to 1.55 range on this item comes from. That study's lower net figure is not used, because it subtracts on-farm carbon sequestration and composting credits that almost no other food study takes. Avocado moves by refrigerated ship, not by plane, so there is no air-freight penalty in this number -- water use, not carbon, is avocado's real environmental story. Avocado oil is a separate product with a much higher figure, so do not log it here.

items.calculation_notes: This figure comes from Agribalyse, the French environmental agency ADEME's food database, and is specifically its sea-freighted row for raw mango pulp: the number assumes the fruit arrived by refrigerated ship. Agribalyse publishes air-freighted mango as a separate row at 11.6 -- about 16x higher -- and the two rows are identical apart from transport (0.47 by sea against 11.4 by air), with farming at 0.15 either way, just 2% of the air-freighted total. In other words, nothing a mango grower does matters next to whether the fruit got on a plane, which is why the range on this item runs from 0.728 all the way to 11.6. We show one entry at the sea value because a shopper cannot tell from the fruit how it travelled and refrigerated sea is the dominant mode, but if you know your mango was air-freighted, the true figure is far higher. The basis is edible flesh, stone and skin excluded, so weigh the flesh: a whole 473 g mango entered here would overstate by about 1.4x. Two independent checks, neither used as a value: the US National Mango Board's baseline assessment gives 0.4556 kg CO2e per kg from production to US retail distribution centres on whole fruit -- a narrower boundary, and industry-commissioned rather than peer-reviewed -- and a 2025 study finds air freight around 30x sea per kg of fruit against Agribalyse's 24x on the transport stage. Because Agribalyse measures to the consumer and counts only direct land-use change, its numbers should not be read against the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for most produce here.

items.calculation_notes: Derived, not measured: raisins are dried grapes, so we take Poore & Nemecek 2018's global average for their whole 'Berries & Grapes' group (1.53, including land-use change and supply-chain losses) and scale it up for the water lost in drying. That underlying 1.53 is itself a group average, not a measurement of raisins or of any one grape variety. Grapes are about 80.5% water and seedless raisins about 15.4% by USDA composition data, and dry matter is conserved through drying, so it takes roughly 4.35 kg of fresh grapes to make 1 kg of raisins: 1.53 x 4.35 gives about 6.65. Two published drying ratios bracket that independently -- UC Cooperative Extension gives 4.1 to 4.5 to 1, and Iowa State's Agricultural Marketing Resource Center gives 4 to 4.5 pounds of green grapes per pound of raisins. No extra energy is added for the drying itself, because most raisins are sun-dried on trays in the vineyard rather than run through a heated evaporator. The basis is the dried weight, so weigh the raisins themselves, not the grapes they came from. Moisture varies: USDA's own range for raisins (9.9% to 22.5% water) implies 6.09 to 7.08, and at the Codex standard's 18% moisture ceiling it works out to 6.45 -- narrow enough that a single number is fair. Sultanas log here too; the Codex raisin standard covers them but excludes dried currants, which are a different dried vine fruit.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. The figure is per kg of dry roasted grounds, not per kg or litre of made coffee -- Poore & Nemecek's own unit is 1 kg of ground, roasted beans, so green beans are not the basis. Chart value 28.53; supply-chain stage sum 28.5279. Coffee is drunk about 10 g at a time, so the per-cup amount is the meaningful scale: 10 x 28.53 / 1000 = 0.2853 kg CO2e for a mug, 0.20 kg for a 7 g filter cup and 0.51 kg for an 18 g double espresso. Those sit just under published per-cup estimates of roughly 0.3-0.4 kg, which are quoted at a larger dose -- at Poore & Nemecek's own 15 g serving the figure is 0.428 kg. This is why coffee is logged by the cup and not by weight: entering 250 g because a mug holds 250 ml would compute 7.13 kg CO2e, tens of times the real amount. For the same reason it is kept out of any 'worst food' ranking -- a per-kg figure for a 10 g dose misleads. Green-bean studies (about 15.33 per kg, Nab & Maslin) sit below this because roasting mass loss and supply-chain losses are not yet applied. Boiling the kettle is not included, here or anywhere in this dataset. The 7, 10 and 18 g cup weights follow Specialty Coffee Association brewing guidance -- the lower end and the midpoint of its Golden Cup ratio, and the standard double espresso basket.

items.calculation_notes: Derived from the coffee figure using a published trade standard rather than an estimate, and it is per kg of dry soluble powder, not per kg or litre of made coffee. The International Coffee Organization's green-bean-equivalent conversions put 1 kg of soluble coffee at 2.6 kg of green beans and 1 kg of roasted coffee at 1.19, so 1 kg of soluble powder takes about 2.18 kg of roasted coffee (2.6 / 1.19), and 28.53 x 2.6 / 1.19 = 62.33 is the figure stored here. That derivation only works because the coffee row is measured on roasted beans; read on green beans it would instead give 74.18. Treat 62.33 as a floor rather than a central estimate: the extraction, concentration and spray- or freeze-drying energy that turns brewed coffee into powder is not added, so the number errs low. A spoonful of instant makes a mug from far less material than ground coffee does, so per cup instant is not necessarily the worse choice: 1.8 x 62.33 / 1000 = 0.112 kg CO2e per mug against 0.285 kg for a 10 g cup of ground coffee, about 61% lower per cup even though the per-kg number is 2.2x taller. The per-kg figure on its own would mislead, which is also why every cup label carries its gram weight: 'one cup' means 10 g of grounds but only about 1.8 g of powder, a 5.6x difference behind identical words. The 1.8 g mug is Nescafe's own serving guidance (1.8 g, about a teaspoon, in a 200 ml mug, with a 100 g jar making roughly 55 mugs), and the 1 g and 2 g presets are USDA portion records for a teaspoon and a sachet. There is no usable independent figure to check this against: the one database with ready-to-drink coffee rows contradicts its own dry-coffee row -- its instant drink implies about 165 kg CO2e per kg of powder, some twenty times its own ground-coffee value -- so it is not used in either direction. Boiling the kettle is not included.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek do not cover tea, so this is an assembled average of four independent tea life-cycle studies with the water-boiling stage removed, not a figure read from a single source: Darjeeling 8.70 (Doublet & Jungbluth 2010), Darjeeling 8.90 (Cichorowski et al. 2015), Chinese organic teas 12.42 (Xu et al. 2019) and South Indian 6.13 (Premalatha et al. 2024) average to 9.04, rounded to 9.0. It covers green and black tea and is per kg of dry leaf, not per kg or litre of brewed tea, and it carries no land-use-change term because none of the underlying studies model one. The spread behind the average is wide: Kenyan tea sits around 2.0 and Sri Lankan orthodox tea around 21.6. A Japanese sencha study (Masuda & Tomioka 2011, Shiga) at 6.28 for flat land and 8.51 for mountain cultivation falls comfortably inside it. Boiling water at home is excluded here, as it is for every item in this dataset, which is why published per-cup tea figures -- mostly kettle energy -- are far larger. Tea is drunk 2-3 g at a time, so the per-cup amount is the meaningful scale and tea is logged by the cup: 2 x 9.0 / 1000 = 0.018 kg CO2e for a tea bag and 3 x 9.0 / 1000 = 0.027 kg for a 3 g mug of loose leaf. For the same reason it is kept out of any 'worst food' ranking. The 2 g tea bag follows the international tea-brewing standard of 2 g per 100 ml (ISO 3103) and the 3 g loose-leaf mug follows Japanese sencha guidance. Matcha carries this same number, so a difference between tea and matcha here is not a real one. Weighed as: leaves.

items.calculation_notes: This is the tea average applied to matcha, not a measurement of matcha, and it is per kg of dry ground leaf rather than per bowl of made tea. Matcha is dry Camellia sinensis leaf -- shade-grown tencha, stone-milled -- so it genuinely belongs to the group the tea figure describes, and it carries that 9.0 unchanged. No life-cycle study of matcha or tencha exists: Japanese journal archives, the agriculture ministry's 2021 tea report and the general literature all return nothing, and that ministry report describes shade cultivation without ever giving a per-kg emissions figure. Every 'matcha carbon footprint' number on the open web traces back to a retailer restating the tea figure, so none of them is used here. Read 9.0 as a floor rather than a central estimate: matcha is whole leaf, shade-grown and drunk in its entirety rather than infused and discarded, and shading for tencha takes materially more nitrogen fertiliser than open-field sencha -- fertiliser N2O is already the largest single contributor in the Japanese tea study behind this figure, at 36-38% -- while stone-milling energy is not modelled at all. The tea average does not resolve any of that. A bowl of usucha is a 2 g dose, so matcha is logged by the bowl: 2 x 9.0 / 1000 = 0.018 kg CO2e, identical to a tea bag because it is the same number, and a difference between matcha and tea here is not a real one. Whisking water is excluded, as boiling is for every item here. The 2 g usucha weight comes from Ippodo Tea's basic usucha method (2 g of matcha to 60 ml of water at 80 degrees C); the 4 g koicha bowl is simply twice that dose rather than a separately sourced weight. Weighed as: whole leaf, ground.

items.calculation_notes: This is a single modelled value from the French Agribalyse database -- its unsweetened instant cocoa powder entry, row 18100 -- and not an average measured across farms. It is per kg of dry powder, not per mug of made cocoa, and the hot water or milk you mix it into is not part of the figure. Almost all of it is land-use change: 24.3 of the 29.1 total, about 84%, which is deforestation-linked cocoa land, so where the cocoa was grown moves this number enormously. The same pattern is visible inside that database: its dark chocolate bar above 70% cocoa is 19.1 with 16.5 of that from land use, putting the powder about 52% above the bar -- the physically right direction, since powder is close to pure non-fat cocoa solids while a bar is diluted with sugar and cocoa butter. Because it comes from a different database, this figure should not be read against the Poore & Nemecek items that make up most of this dataset: on dark chocolate, the one product both cover, Agribalyse says 19.1 and Poore & Nemecek say 46.65, about 2.4x apart, so the two agree on the story and not on the value. In particular, cocoa powder at 29.1 landing within 2% of coffee at 28.53 is two different accounting boundaries coinciding, not a tie -- measured on a common boundary cocoa powder would be well above coffee. Realistic use is a spoonful, so cocoa is logged by the spoon: 5.4 x 29.1 / 1000 = 0.157 kg CO2e per tablespoon and 0.314 kg for a two-spoon mug, with both spoon weights from USDA portion records. The 86 g preset is a baking quantity rather than a drink and computes 2.50 kg CO2e.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses, measured per litre of soy milk -- drinks here carry a density of 1.0, so per litre and per kg are the same number. Poore & Nemecek's own unit is 1 litre of soymilk at roughly 3.3% protein, so how far the drink is diluted is already built in, and the litre covers growing the beans, processing, transport and packaging. Three readings agree: the per-kg chart gives 0.98, the plant-milk comparison chart gives 0.98 per litre, and the study's own text gives about 1.0 per litre. Soy milk is logged by the glass because nobody weighs a drink: 0.196 kg CO2e for 200 ml, 0.245 kg for 250 ml and 0.98 kg for a 1 litre carton. On the same plant-milk chart almond is 0.70, oat 0.90, soy 0.98 and rice 1.18 per litre, all far below dairy milk at 3.15, but soy and oat are only about 8.5% apart -- close enough that a difference between those two is not meaningful. A home-made or barista version with its own bean-to-water ratio will not match this figure. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek mean taken from Our World in Data's plant-milk comparison chart -- the same chart that supplies oat and rice milk, so the four are measured the same way and can be read against each other. It is per litre of almond milk; drinks here carry a density of 1.0, so per litre and per kg are the same number, and the litre covers growing, processing, transport and packaging. Almond milk is logged by the glass because nobody weighs a drink: 0.140 kg CO2e for 200 ml, 0.176 kg for 250 ml and 0.702 kg for a 1 litre carton. It has the lowest carbon footprint of the plant milks on that chart (almond 0.70, oat 0.90, soy 0.98, rice 1.18 per litre, against dairy milk at 3.15), though oat and soy are only about 8.5% apart and a difference between those two is not meaningful. Carbon is not the whole story: the same chart measures freshwater use in litres per litre, and almond is by far the thirstiest of the plant milks at 371 against rice 270, oat 48 and soy 28 -- roughly 8x oat and 13x soy -- yet still about 41% below dairy milk at 628. So almond milk is the best plant milk on the measure this calculator uses, and the heaviest water user among the plant milks while remaining well below dairy on water too. A home-made or barista version with its own almond-to-water ratio will not match this figure. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: Beer is 1.2 kg CO2e per litre, and because beer is close enough to water in density, a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. This is derived rather than read straight off a published beer figure: Poore & Nemecek 2018 report 0.24 kg CO2e per unit of alcohol, where a unit is 10 ml of pure alcohol, so at 5% ABV one unit is 200 ml of beer and 0.24 divided by 0.2 litres gives 1.2 per litre. Their own functional unit for the barley row is one litre of beer, so this is a beverage figure and not a grain one. Because it comes from their per-unit table rather than their headline chart, it may not carry the supply-chain-losses uplift the chart values include; dedicated studies of packaged beer land lower, around 0.51 to 0.84 per litre, which is context on the spread rather than a correction to this number. Cider logs here too -- the one database that measures cider and beer on the same boundary separates them by about 1.5% (1.35 against 1.33), so a difference between them here would not be real. Watch the loanwords: Spanish sidra is alcoholic cider and belongs here, but Japanese サイダー is a clear fizzy lemonade and belongs on the cola and fizzy drink entry instead. Per serving that is about 0.40 kg for a 330 ml can, 0.42 kg for a 350 ml can, 0.57 kg for a 473 ml US pint and 0.60 kg for a 500 ml bottle or long can; 330 ml is the European standard can, 350 ml the most common Japanese can, and 500 ml the size the Japanese health ministry's alcohol guideline uses. Wine looks worse than beer per litre (1.79 against 1.20), but that reverses at the servings people actually pour: a 330 ml can is 0.40 kg against 0.31 kg for a 175 ml glass of wine, so compare these drinks by the can or the glass, not by the litre. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for wine, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses; wine is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. Their separate per-alcohol-unit table gives a cross-check that lands in the same place: 0.14 kg per unit at 12.5% ABV, where a unit is 10 ml of alcohol and so 80 ml of wine, works out at 1.75 per litre, and their functional unit for the wine-grape row is one litre of wine, so this is a beverage figure and not a grape one. The 1.79 used here is the published value with losses included. A 750 ml bottle is about 1.34 kg, which sits inside the 0.06 to 3.0 kg per bottle range a 2024 Nature Communications Earth & Environment study reports across farming systems. Sparkling wine, champagne, cava and prosecco are not covered here: the one database that measures still and sparkling on the same boundary puts sparkling around 43% above dry white and 69% above red, so reading them against this figure understates them by roughly 40% -- log them as Sparkling wine. Per serving that is about 0.22 kg for a 125 ml small glass, 0.27 kg for a 150 ml glass, 0.31 kg for a 175 ml standard glass and 1.34 kg for a whole bottle; the 175 ml glass comes from the NHS alcohol-unit table and the 150 ml pour from the US NIAAA standard drink, while the 125 ml measure is a UK convention with no primary source behind it yet. Wine is higher than beer per litre but lower per drink -- a 175 ml glass is 0.31 kg against 0.40 kg for a 330 ml can -- so compare these by the glass or can rather than by the litre. Sake and sparkling wine are each built from a different source on a different boundary, so neither is a fair comparison against this number. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: This is a single modelled value for white sparkling wine from the French Agribalyse database, not a mean across producers, so it carries no published spread. Sparkling wine is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. Within that one database, and so on one consistent boundary, sparkling sits well above still wine: red 1.27, rose 1.46, dry white 1.50, white sparkling 2.14 and champagne 2.23 -- about 43% above dry white and 69% above red, driven mainly by the heavy pressure-rated bottle rather than by the grapes. Champagne logs here too, since it comes out within about 4% of this figure. Because this figure comes from a different database than the Poore & Nemecek values used for still wine, beer and most other items, it should not be read against them: Agribalyse runs roughly a third to a half of the Poore & Nemecek scale for the same foods, so 2.14 here and 1.79 on still wine are not on the same basis and the gap between them is not a measured difference. Per serving that is about 0.27 kg for a 125 ml flute, 0.32 kg for a 150 ml glass and 1.61 kg for a 750 ml bottle; the 150 ml pour is the US NIAAA standard drink and 750 ml the standard bottle, while the flute size is a convention with no primary source behind it yet. items.calculation_notes: Sake has no usable published life-cycle figure of its own, so this is derived from rice. Japan's National Tax Agency reports national production of 321,752 kL of sake from 119,833 tonnes of white rice, which is about 0.372 kg of milled rice per litre of sake; multiplied by Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for rice (4.45) that gives about 1.66 kg CO2e per litre, and sake is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. Read 1.66 as a floor rather than a central estimate, because it covers the rice and nothing else: brewing and koji energy are not in it, nor is the distilling alcohol added at around 50 ml of pure alcohol per litre nationally (itself an agricultural product with its own footprint), nor the heavy 720 ml and 1.8 litre glass bottles sake ships in -- packaging alone is 59 to 77% of a soft drink's total -- nor distribution. The upper end of the range, about 2.66, comes from counting the brown rice that went into the mill (192,377 tonnes) instead of the white rice that came out, so the 1.66 to 2.66 spread is really a question of the polishing ratio -- how much of each grain is milled away, and who carries that loss. The figure here uses white rice because Poore & Nemecek's rice row is milled rice as sold. Two alternatives were ruled out: the Agribalyse database's sake value is identical to its vodka, whisky, rum, brandy and pure-alcohol values -- one proxy standing behind six labels, and it puts 40% spirits below 5% beer, which distillation makes impossible -- and the one dedicated brewery study we found is paywalled, so no number was taken from it. Per serving that is about 0.10 kg for a 60 ml glass, 0.30 kg for a 180 ml gō and 1.19 kg for a 720 ml bottle, each of them a floor in the same way; the gō comes from the Japanese health ministry's alcohol guideline and the 720 ml bottle is four gō, while the 60 ml pour is a third of a gō with no primary source behind it. Because this is built by a different route and is a floor rather than a mean, it and the wine figure are not a fair comparison. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.
