items.calculation_notes: This comes from a single case study of one Irish single malt distillery. One distillery is a thin basis, and this figure may not represent whisky, vodka, gin and rum generally. That study reports 2.26 kg CO2e per litre of pure alcohol; a litre of 40% ABV spirit holds 0.4 litres of alcohol, so 2.26 x 0.4 gives 0.904 kg CO2e per litre of bottled spirit -- and spirits are close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. 40% is the minimum strength the EU and US spirit-drink definitions set for these drinks and the strength the NHS alcohol-unit table assumes. The study stops at the distillery gate: barley growing and distilling energy are about 90% of what it counts, and the glass bottle and distribution are not in it at all. That is why 0.904 per litre lands below beer's 1.20, which looks surprising and is the wrong way round -- a spirits bottle weighing around 500 g is roughly a third to a half of a real packaged footprint, and adding it back would put spirits near or above wine per litre. Treat the per-litre figure as a floor and do not read it against beer or wine. Per drink the picture holds however the packaging gap falls: a 25 ml single is about 0.023 kg against 0.40 kg for a 330 ml beer and 0.31 kg for a 175 ml glass of wine, 14 to 17 times smaller, and even if packaging doubled this factor a single would still be 7 to 9 times smaller. Per serving: about 0.023 kg for a 25 ml single, 0.032 kg for a 35 ml large measure, 0.040 kg for a 44 ml shot and 0.054 kg for a 60 ml double; the 25 ml and 35 ml measures come from the NHS unit table and 44 ml is the 1.5 fl oz US standard drink, while the 60 ml Japanese bar double has no primary source behind it. Shochu logs here as well, but at 20 to 25% ABV rather than 40% its real per-serving figures are roughly half of these. The Agribalyse database was no help either: its spirits value is a single proxy shared with sake and pure alcohol, and it too puts 40% spirits below 5% beer. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: This is a single modelled value for sugared cola from the French Agribalyse database, covering the chain from farm to consumer, and it is one modelled product rather than a mean across producers, so it carries no published spread. A fizzy drink is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. Diet cola, sweetener-only and caffeine-free colas and plain lemonade all return this same value in that database, so they log here too and a difference between them is not real. One honest limitation: the packaging in this figure is not a declared container but a proxy inventory, so 0.493 is an average retail mix rather than 'a can' -- and that matters because packaging is most of the number. A 2013 study of carbonated soft drinks in the International Journal of Life Cycle Assessment puts packaging at 59 to 77% of the total, with a 2 litre PET bottle the best option and glass the worst; a glass bottle reused three times comes level with an aluminium can or a 0.5 litre PET, so a glass bottle is materially worse than this figure and a 2 litre PET materially better. Energy drinks are not the same product: the same database on the same boundary puts a sugared energy drink at 0.685, so this figure understates one by around 28%. Watch the loanwords -- Japanese サイダー is a clear fizzy drink and belongs here, while Spanish sidra is alcoholic cider and belongs on the beer entry. Per serving that is about 0.16 kg for a 330 ml can, 0.18 kg for a 360 ml large can and 0.25 kg for a 500 ml bottle; 330 ml is the European standard can, 360 ml is the 12 fl oz US reference amount for beverages and 500 ml the standard single-serve bottle. This comes from a different database than the Poore & Nemecek figures used for most items and should not be read against them -- Agribalyse runs roughly a third to a half of the Poore & Nemecek scale for the same foods. Apple juice, from this same database, is 0.567 against cola's 0.493, which is too close to call a winner. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: This is a modelled value from the French Agribalyse database for orange juice reconstituted from concentrate -- one modelled product, not a mean across producers. Orange juice is close enough to water in density that a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. The recorded range runs from 0.906 to 1.6, and what drives it is whether the juice travelled as concentrate or as juice: the same database puts home-squeezed, not-from-concentrate orange juice at 1.6, because squeezing your own from whole oranges takes the same fruit but ships the water. Apple juice is kept separate rather than folded in here: on the same boundary in the same database, pure apple juice is 0.567, about 60% below packaged orange juice and nearly three times below the home-squeezed figure. Because this comes from a different database than the Poore & Nemecek figures used for most items, it should not be read against them -- Agribalyse runs roughly a third to a half of the Poore & Nemecek scale for the same foods. items.calculation_notes: This is a single modelled value from the French Agribalyse database for a plain, pre-packed coconut drink -- the carton you pour and drink, not a tin of cooking coconut milk and not coconut water. It is a diluted coconut milk drink, typically only around 5% coconut extract with the rest water, so being essentially water a litre and a kilogram are the same entry here. That database also holds a coconut water row at 0.836 which confusingly carries an identical French product name, so this entry was identified by its English name to be sure it is the drink rather than the water. It is one modelled product rather than a mean across producers, so it carries no published spread; land-use change is included and makes up about 0.2 of the total. Coconut milk for cooking is a separate entry on a different basis -- per 100 g as packed, not per litre as poured -- so if you are looking at a tin, use that one. There is an inconsistency worth knowing about: in this same database the concentrated cooking product comes out at 0.682, below the 1.21 here, meaning a drink that is mostly water is modelled 77% higher per litre than its own concentrate. Both cannot be right, and the two rows use proxy packaging with different data-quality ratings, so the drink and the tin should not be read against each other. Per serving that is about 0.24 kg for a 200 ml glass, 0.30 kg for a 250 ml large glass and 1.21 kg for a 1 litre carton; the 200 ml and 250 ml glasses are the same measures used for dairy, soy and oat milk. Because this comes from a different database than the Poore & Nemecek figures used for most items, it should not be read against them -- Agribalyse runs roughly a third to a half of the Poore & Nemecek scale for the same foods. Weighed as: liquid, density 1.0 -- per litre = per kg.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for dark chocolate, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Their functional unit is 1 kg of dark chocolate, so this is the finished bar rather than cocoa solids, and because the study never states the recipe no cocoa-solids figure can be pulled back out of it. Land-use change is about 26 of the 46.65 -- roughly 55% of the total -- and it is almost all deforestation for cocoa, which is why sourcing can move chocolate from near-zero to over 46. The figure of about 19 that circulates widely is the same study's median without supply-chain losses, not this mean. Milk chocolate has its own figure (14.9) -- log it as Milk chocolate -- but do not read the roughly 3x gap as a reason to switch: the two numbers come from different studies drawn on different boundaries, so most of that gap is an accounting artefact rather than a measured difference in how the two are made. Weigh the chocolate as bought; the 12.6 g square preset is one eighth of a standard 101 g bar.

items.calculation_notes: This one does not come from Poore & Nemecek like most foods here: it is a single UK study of chocolate production and consumption (Konstantas and colleagues, 2018), specifically their case that includes land-use change from growing cocoa. That inclusion is the whole number -- their no-land-use-change case is only 3.4, so deforestation-linked cocoa is three to four times everything else put together. The study does publish the recipe Poore & Nemecek never state: 45% sugar, 24.5% milk powder, 17% cocoa butter, 8% cocoa liquor, 5% vegetable fat and 0.5% emulsifiers, so 25% cocoa solids. Because it is a different source on a different boundary from the dark chocolate figure (46.65), the roughly 3x gap between the two is partly an accounting artefact rather than a measured difference, and it is not a reason to switch to milk chocolate. Rebuilding this same recipe using Poore & Nemecek's own cocoa arithmetic gives 23.8 rather than 14.9 -- the two sources disagree by two to three times on cocoa itself, the ingredient that dominates both -- so treat 14.9 as the low end of a 14.9 to 23.8 range rather than a central estimate. Two further caveats: the study is cradle-to-grave, so it counts home use and packaging disposal that the rest of this dataset stops short of, and its cocoa land-use-change data (UK government, 2009) is one the authors themselves say to treat with caution. Weigh the chocolate as bought; the 12.6 g square preset is borrowed from a standard 101 g dark-chocolate bar.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 publish cane sugar and beet sugar separately -- 3.20 and 1.81 kg CO2e per kg, both for 1 kg of raw or refined sugar, including land-use change and supply-chain losses -- and a bag of white sugar does not tell you which crop it came from (European sugar is mostly beet, tropical sugar mostly cane, and Japanese 上白糖 and グラニュー糖 are a mix). So this is a production-weighted blend of the two: cane is about 80% of world sugar and beet about 20% (European Commission figures, matched independently by the World Sugar Research Organisation), giving 0.80 x 3.20 + 0.20 x 1.81 = 2.92. The two rows differ almost entirely because of land-use change, which is around 39% of the cane figure and essentially nil for beet. That makes the blend deliberately wrong for any one place: a European shopper's real figure is nearer the all-beet 1.81 and a tropical shopper's nearer the all-cane 3.20, and anything that names its crop -- demerara, muscovado, or a bag labelled 'cane sugar' -- sits at the 3.20 end. Sugar, sweets and crisps land within a few percent of each other, with jam not far below, so the ordering between them is not meaningful. Weigh the sugar as bought.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 have no crisps row, so this is built from their potato and sunflower oil figures, both of which include land-use change and supply-chain losses. A peer-reviewed inventory of potato-chip production uses 0.2 kg of harvested potatoes for a 50 g bag, which is about 4 kg of potatoes per kg of crisps, and Japanese composition tables put crisps at 34.2 g of fat per 100 g, so about 0.34 kg of frying oil per kg -- a fat measurement rather than an oil-volume assumption. That gives 4.0 x 0.46 for the potatoes plus 0.34 x 3.60 for the oil: about 1.84 + 1.23 = 3.07 kg CO2e per kg. Only the ingredients are counted -- the factory's frying energy and the bag are not -- so read this as a floor rather than a complete figure. The frying oil carries the whole uncertainty: sunflower gives this 3.07, rapeseed about 3.13 and palm about 4.34, and since the composition table does not name the oil, sunflower is assumed and declared. That same potato-chip study's own full cradle-to-grave total is 1.96 kg CO2e per kg, which is less than its ingredients alone cost on Poore & Nemecek's figures -- a familiar gap between European database numbers and that study -- so it is not used here, though its oil input (about 0.31 kg per kg) agrees with the composition figure to within 10%. Sugar, sweets and crisps land within a few percent of each other, with jam not far below, so the ordering between them is not meaningful. Weigh the crisps as bought: the 50 g bag is the study's own unit, and the 30 g and 28 g presets come from the US snack serving standard, which names potato chips directly. In Spanish, 'patatas fritas' can also mean hot chips; this item is the bagged snack.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 have no popcorn row, so this is built from their maize figure plus frying oil, with Japanese composition tables used to work out how much of each is in the finished snack. Popcorn is 4% water and 21.7% fat; maize grain is 14.5% water and 4.5% fat; matching the non-fat solids on both sides gives about 0.92 kg of maize per kg of popcorn, and subtracting the fat the maize itself brings leaves about 0.18 kg of added oil per kg. That is 0.92 x 1.70 for the maize plus 0.18 x 3.60 for the oil: about 1.56 + 0.63 = 2.19 kg CO2e per kg, land-use change and supply-chain losses included in both parents. The basis is popped, oil-popped weight -- popped and unpopped kernels differ several-fold by weight, so weigh the popcorn after popping, not the kernels in the bag. Only the ingredients are counted; popping at a factory and the packaging are not, so this is a floor. Air-popped popcorn works out at about 1.91, since it carries no added oil and so needs slightly more than its own weight in maize, and palm frying oil would push the figure to about 2.85. Cinema popcorn with a butter topping sits above that whole range and is not this item. Jam and popcorn are close enough together that the ordering between them is not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: No life-cycle study of confectionery is available, so this is derived from sugar: a boiled sweet is sugar and water and nothing else -- Japanese composition tables put fruit drops at 2% water with no fat and no protein -- so about 0.98 kg of sugar per kg of sweets, and 0.98 x 2.92 = 2.86 kg CO2e per kg. The sugar figure behind it is a blend of Poore & Nemecek 2018's cane and beet rows, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Only the sugar is counted: boiling, moulding and the wrapper are not, so it is understated on that side. On the other side, treating every gram of dry matter as cane or beet sugar is an upper bound, because real sweets use a lot of glucose and corn syrup, which carry less (corn syrup around 2.5 and high-fructose corn syrup around 1.0, against 2.92 for sugar) -- a half-and-half sweet would come out near 2.66, so the honest range is roughly 2.64 to 2.86 and the number here is its top end. Gummies and jelly beans log here too: jelly beans hold more water and work out about 8% lower, which is too small a difference to justify a separate figure, and the gelatin in gummies is not modelled and pushes the other way. Sugar, sweets and crisps land within a few percent of each other, with jam not far below, so the ordering between them is not meaningful. Weigh the sweets as bought.

items.calculation_notes: This is the midpoint of a peer-reviewed study's own range, 0.67 to 0.92 kg CO2e per kg, giving 0.795. Two caveats matter. First, that study stops at processed honey with no packaging and no transport to the shop, which is a shorter chain than the rest of this dataset, so treat 0.795 as a floor rather than a like-for-like figure. Second, published values for honey run from 0.38 to 2.5 kg CO2e per kg -- a 6.6x spread -- driven almost entirely by whether hives are trucked between crops and whether the bees are fed supplementary sugar. Migratory beekeeping lands around 1.4 to 2.2; stationary hives around 0.38 to 0.48. Because of that spread, honey is not used in generated comparisons. A spoonful is 21 g, from the US Department of Agriculture's own portion data, which works out to about 17 g CO2e.

items.calculation_notes: Worked out from the EU jam directive rather than measured directly, so it is a recipe rather than a product test. The regulation sets a minimum of 450 g of fruit and at least 600 g of soluble dry matter per kilogram of finished jam, which implies 555 g of added sugar; costing those two legs against this dataset's own berry and sugar figures gives 2.31. Three things to know. This is the LEGAL MINIMUM fruit content, so a premium jam with more fruit and a reduced-sugar jam sit either side of it. The fruit leg uses Poore & Nemecek's whole 'Berries & Grapes' category, not a strawberry measurement, so this is best read as a strawberry-style archetype -- an apricot or apple jam would come out slightly lower. And the jar and the boiling are not counted, so the real figure is a little higher. The 2001 version of the same directive would give 2.19, which is why the directive version is pinned. A spoonful is 20 g, about 46 g CO2e.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 measure oils per litre of refined oil rather than per kilogram, so their published figures have to be converted before they can be used against a weight. This item is the average of their sunflower and rapeseed oils, each converted separately: sunflower at about 3.60 per litre divided by a density of about 0.919 kg per litre gives about 3.92 per kg, rapeseed at about 3.77 per litre divided by about 0.915 gives about 4.12 per kg, and the two average to the 4.02 shown here. Those densities are Codex Alimentarius relative densities at 20C; USDA and Japanese (MEXT) composition tables put the same two oils between 0.913 and 0.921 kg per litre, so which reference table you use barely moves the answer. Sunflower and rapeseed are only about 5% apart and share this one number, so a difference between them here is not real, and a specific bottle may sit anywhere between roughly 3.92 and 4.12. Sesame oil logs here too, and this is not a measurement of sesame: Poore & Nemecek have no sesame row at all, and in the Agribalyse database sesame oil shares its farming and refining stages digit-for-digit with rapeseed oil, with the entire difference sitting in packaging and transport -- it is the rapeseed inventory in a different bottle. Codex gives sesame essentially the same density, so this figure is a defensible stand-in for it rather than a sesame measurement. Agribalyse independently puts sunflower and rapeseed together at the bottom of its oils, which supports that ranking but not the value: its numbers run about 0.6x these. Coconut oil in this list sits at 4.15 and looks almost identical, but that comes from a different database and the near-tie is a coincidence -- measured on the same Agribalyse basis, coconut oil is about 66% above rapeseed. Everything here is a global mean from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Weigh the oil as poured; the spoon presets assume about 0.917 g per ml, so a 15 ml spoonful is about 13.8 g.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 measure oils per litre of refined oil rather than per kilogram, and olive oil appears only in their stage-by-stage breakdown, which totals about 5.42 per litre. Converting that to a weight uses the density implied by USDA composition data for olive oil -- 1 tablespoon at 13.5 g, or about 0.913 kg per litre, which the teaspoon and cup portions of the same record agree with exactly and the Japanese (MEXT) table matches to within 0.33% -- so about 5.42 divided by about 0.913 gives the 5.94 per kg shown here, roughly 9.5% above the published per-litre figure. This is a global mean from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Land-use change is a small credit here rather than a cost, about -0.32, or -6% of the total, because olive groves store carbon as they grow. Olive and palm oil are not a fair comparison: the ordering between them depends on where the boundary is drawn and reverses if you count production alone. Weigh the oil as poured.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 measure oils per litre of refined oil rather than per kilogram, so this item averages their palm and soybean oils after converting each to a weight basis: soybean at about 6.32 per litre divided by a density of about 0.920 kg per litre gives about 6.87 per kg, palm at about 7.32 per litre divided by about 0.900 gives about 8.13 per kg, and the two average to the 7.50 shown here. The soybean density is a Codex Alimentarius relative density at 20C. The palm density comes from the Japanese (MEXT) composition table for refined palm oil, and it is the weakest number in this entry: refined palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature, so Codex can only quote it warm -- at 50C for palm oil and 40C for palm olein, the liquid cooking fraction -- and because oil gets denser as it cools, neither of those can be used directly. A litre of palm oil is not really a well-defined quantity in a kitchen, which is a caveat on measuring oil by volume rather than on the arithmetic. USDA composition data puts both oils nearer 0.921 kg per litre, which would pull the result down a little. Palm and soybean are about 18% apart and share this one number, so a difference between them here is not real and a specific bottle may sit anywhere between roughly 6.87 and 8.13 -- palm on its own would be about 8.13, not the 7.32 that appears as a per-litre figure elsewhere. Grouping the two is more than arithmetic: land-use change is about 38% of the palm figure and about 45% of the soybean figure, against roughly 3% for sunflower, 5% for rapeseed and a small credit for olive, so these are the two oils whose emissions are dominated by clearing land. On a production-only boundary, counting neither land-use change nor the supply chain, both fall to roughly 2.2 and the ordering against olive oil can reverse, so palm and olive are not a fair comparison. The Agribalyse database also puts palm and soy at the top of its own oils, which supports that ranking, though it disagrees on the gap between the two -- about 64% there against about 18% here. Figures are a global mean from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Weigh the oil as poured; the spoon presets assume about 0.910 g per ml, so a 15 ml spoonful is about 13.7 g.

items.calculation_notes: Mayonnaise is built up from a named product's declared ingredient percentages rather than measured directly: Hellmann's Real Mayonnaise in its UK and EU recipe lists rapeseed oil at 78% and pasteurised egg and egg yolk at 7.9%, so 0.78 x the vegetable oil figure of 4.02 gives 3.13, 0.079 x Poore & Nemecek's 4.67 for eggs gives 0.37, and the total is the 3.50 shown here. Those two ingredients are only about 86% of the jar -- the vinegar, salt, sugar and minor sunflower oil carry no declared percentage and are not counted -- so read 3.50 as 'at least', not as a central estimate. As a check, the US standard of identity requires mayonnaise to be at least 65% vegetable oil, which sets a bare floor of about 2.61, and 3.50 clears that with about a third to spare. Two lower published figures are rejected against that floor: a 1.46 that circulates in other emissions datasets, which falls below even the bare regulatory minimum, and Agribalyse's mayonnaise entry at about 2.68, which sits below this recipe calculation and only a couple of percent above the floor. Because the number rests on one recipe, it forks by market, and the forks are not averaged: the UK and EU line shown here is the only one with a declared oil percentage, a US jar made with soybean oil works out at about 5.73, roughly 64% higher, and Japanese mayonnaise, made with a rapeseed, corn and soybean blend, sits between the two. The Japanese (MEXT) composition table supports the ratio, putting whole-egg mayonnaise at 76 g of fat per 100 g -- that includes the fat from the egg yolk, so the oil alone is a little under it, close to Hellmann's 78%. The oil figure behind this carries a conversion from Poore & Nemecek's per-litre basis to a weight (see the vegetable oil entry), while their egg figure is already per kilogram; both are global means from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Mayonnaise, margarine and ketchup all land close together, between about 3.1 and 3.5, and because each is built up from its declared recipe rather than measured, the ordering between them is not meaningful; mayonnaise is mostly the same seed oil, so it is not independent of the vegetable oil figure either. The presets are the weight of the product as bought, and the manufacturer's own declared portion is 15 g.

items.calculation_notes: This comes from Agribalyse, the French public food-emissions database, and its 'Soy sauce, prepacked' row -- a different database from Poore & Nemecek 2018, which most other items here use, so this figure should not be read against those numbers; a gap between the two sources is not a real difference. It counts the crop, the brewing, the packaging, the transport and the supermarket, and stops at the shelf: what you do with it in your own kitchen is not included. Soy sauce is a Japanese staple riding a French row, and that is a real gap -- no published per-kilogram life-cycle figure for soy sauce exists from any Japanese source we could reach, and the only Japanese datum we found is Kikkoman's own energy-per-litre-of-production disclosure, which is a factory energy figure rather than a life-cycle study; it lands in roughly the same place as the Agribalyse processing stage, so it is a directional check only and is not used as a value. Packaging is 0.414 of the total, about 42%, so a glass bottle versus a refill pouch moves this figure materially. Soy sauce is denser than water at 1.181 g per ml, so do not assume a millilitre is a gram: a 15 ml spoonful is about 17.7 g. Soy sauce and vinegar are within 3% of each other here, so the ordering between them is not meaningful, and miso comes out about 23% higher, close enough that a data revision could change it.

items.calculation_notes: This is a concentrate figure, and that is the whole point of it: it is the fresh tomatoes it takes to make a kilogram of ketchup, not a kilogram of tomatoes. Heinz Tomato Ketchup (460 g, UK) declares "Tomatoes (148g per 100g Tomato Ketchup)", so 1.48 kg of fresh tomatoes per kg of ketchup, and 1.48 x Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for tomatoes, 2.09, gives 3.09. The concentration checks out against composition tables: fresh tomatoes are about 94% water, so 148 g of them carries about 8.9 g of solids, and ketchup is about 34% solids, leaving roughly 25 g per 100 g of added sugar, salt and vinegar -- consistent with the sugars Heinz declares. Only the tomatoes are counted, so read this as a floor: the added sugar is about 19 g per 100 g inferred from composition rather than declared, and would add somewhere between 0.34 and 0.61 depending on whether it is beet or cane sugar. Agribalyse's own ketchup row (1.18) was not used, because it falls 62% below just the tomato content of the product valued on our own tomato figure. Ketchup is denser than water at 1.15 g per ml, so a 15 ml spoonful is about 17 g, and the 15 g serving is Heinz's own. This figure is brand-specific, and it sits within a few percent of margarine and about 13% from mayonnaise, so the ordering between those three is not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: This is a tomato sauce figure only, built from a named product's declared ingredient percentages: Dolmio Original Sauce for Bolognese (Mars UK, 450 g jar), which declares tomatoes at 83% and double concentrated tomato paste at 7.0%. The paste is converted back to fresh tomatoes using composition tables -- paste is about 28.7% solids against about 6.0% for fresh tomatoes, a ratio of about 4.78 -- so 7% paste is worth about 0.33 kg of fresh tomatoes, and the jar carries about 1.16 kg of fresh-tomato equivalent per kg of sauce. That times Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for tomatoes, 2.09, gives 2.43. The 28.7% solids also puts Dolmio's "double concentrated" paste in the right regulatory band: the Codex standard for processed tomato concentrates defines tomato paste as a concentrate with at least 24% natural total soluble solids. Onion, maize starch, sugar, salt and sunflower oil are declared but not by weight, so they are not counted; they are at most a tenth of the mass and all low-impact, so the understatement is under about 5%. Sugo, marinara and passata log here, but pesto and cream or carbonara sauces do not -- they are far apart in impact and this number would badly misrepresent them. Meat sauces are excluded for the same reason and more sharply: in Agribalyse a prepacked bolognese sauce comes out at 13.2 against 1.47 for a tomato-and-onion sauce, a 9x difference, so logging a jar of bolognese here would tell you a beef product costs the same as a vegetable one. The 112 g portion is Dolmio's own (four per jar) and 125 g is the US Food and Drug Administration's reference amount for main entree sauces such as spaghetti sauce. This figure sits within about 9% of onigiri and close to salsa, so the ordering between them is not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: This is the global average for Poore & Nemecek 2018's whole "Other Vegetables" group -- a catch-all row -- not a measurement of olives. It is their global mean including land-use change and supply-chain losses, and a table olive lands there because it is a fruit eaten as a vegetable and the study has no closer home for it. The basis is drained, so weigh the olives out of the brine: the US Food and Drug Administration's 15 g reference amount for olives is for drained solids. Pitted is a further assumption on our part -- the reference amount does not say -- so read the portions as pitted flesh. This figure almost certainly understates olives, and two independent checks point the same way. Olives are a tree crop pressed for oil at scale, which is a poor fit for a row built from field vegetables: our olive oil figure of 5.95 per kg, at the conventional 5-6 kg of olives per kg of oil, implies fruit at roughly 0.99-1.19 including pressing, about twice this number. And Agribalyse's stuffed green olives total 1.17, of which 0.70 is the glass jar, while the catch-all vegetable row carries only 0.04 of packaging, a field-vegetable profile. Table olives arrive in a jar, and that jar is not in this number, which is why we do not use olives in comparisons with other foods.

items.calculation_notes: This is plain salted onigiri -- no nori, no filling -- because that is what the citable definition covers: Japan's national composition tables define their onigiri entry as 塩むすび, a salt musubi with no seaweed and no filling, containing 0.5 g of salt per 100 g. Japanese labels carry no ingredient percentages, so no convenience-store pack declares its rice, nori and filling masses, and the figure is built by mass balance instead. Polished raw rice is about 85% dry matter and onigiri is about 43%, of which 0.5 g per 100 g is salt, leaving 42.5 g of rice dry matter and so about 50 g of raw rice per 100 g of onigiri. That ratio of about 0.50 against Poore & Nemecek 2018's global mean for rice, 4.45, gives 2.22, plus a negligible 0.003 for the salt from Agribalyse -- 0.14% of the total, from a different database, and it changes nothing. The ratio cross-checks: the same tables put cooked rice at 60% water, which implies rice gains about 213% in weight on cooking, reproducing the official 210% to within about 1.3%. Nori and fillings are left out, and that is the main thing this number misses -- for scale, dried laver in Agribalyse is 11.79 per kg, so a single 1.5 g sheet would add about 0.018, roughly 8%, so a real convenience-store onigiri is a few percent higher than this. Weigh it as bought, cooked and ready-to-eat; the 100 g portion comes from the composition table's 170 kcal per 100 g against Lawson's declared 173 kcal per pack for its 塩にぎり, and Japan's official food balance guide also puts a small bowl of rice at 100 g. Onigiri sits within about 9% of tomato pasta sauce and about 18% of salsa, so the ordering between them is not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: This is Poore & Nemecek 2018's single global average for farmed fish, including land-use change and supply-chain losses -- the same boundary as the meat, dairy and plant items in this app. It is not a measurement of the species you have in mind: one number covers tilapia, basa and pangasius, catfish, carp, and farmed marine fish such as sea bream and sea bass. The honest spread behind it is large -- the same category has been published as low as 5.1 when supply-chain losses are left out, against this 13.63, a 2.7x range -- so the category is strongly skewed and this figure is the conservative reading of it. Poore & Nemecek's own functional unit is 1 kg of edible fish, so weigh the fillet, not the whole fish; a whole fish bought as-purchased will weigh substantially more than its edible portion. Salmon and trout are not covered here and have their own entry: log them as Salmon. A separate seafood meta-analysis puts farmed marine finfish at 11.6 on a narrower boundary, and completing that to this boundary gives 14.23, within about 4% of 13.63, which is the main reason we trust this number. The other seafood items here -- salmon, white fish, tuna and the rest -- come from that meta-analysis and stop at the farm gate, so they sit on a different boundary from this one: salmon reading lower than farmed fish is an accounting difference, not evidence that salmon is cleaner, and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for farmed prawns, Poore & Nemecek 2018, including land-use change and supply-chain losses -- the same boundary and the same kind of average as every meat, dairy and plant item here. Their functional unit is 1 kg of head-free, shell-free meat, so this is an edible-meat figure: weigh peeled prawns, and note that shell-on prawns weigh about 1.18x their peeled meat, so a bag bought as-purchased is more than the edible weight. The other seafood items in this app come from a Bayesian meta-analysis of blue foods, which puts farmed shrimp at 9.43, but that is not a lower version of the same measurement: it stops at the farm gate, its authors state that they exclude methane from ponds and nitrous oxide, and all 79 shrimp records behind it are pond systems, while Poore & Nemecek model pond emissions explicitly (they report 0-450 g of methane per kg of liveweight from freshwater aquaculture ponds). Completing that farm-gate figure to this boundary still only reaches 15.03, so the honest cradle-to-retail band for farmed prawns is about 15 to 27, and this entry uses the published top of that band rather than an assembled number: Poore & Nemecek's crustacean sample has the widest spread in their study (their median is 11.8 against this mean of 26.87), and where the uncertainty is this large we use the figure that does not flatter the choice. Because the two sources draw their boundaries differently, this number and the meta-analysis-sourced seafood items next to it are not a fair comparison in either direction, and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: Wild-caught prawns are not in Poore & Nemecek 2018, which publishes only a farmed prawn category, so this figure is derived. A Bayesian meta-analysis of blue foods (Gephart et al. 2021) publishes both variants at one boundary and puts wild above farmed -- 11.96 against 9.43 per kg of edible weight, wild being 1.27x farmed, because trawling for prawns is among the most fuel-intensive fishing there is -- and that ratio is applied to the Poore & Nemecek farmed prawn figure this app uses: 26.87 x 1.2682 = 34.08. The caveat is that scaling by a ratio also scales feed and land-use-change stages a wild fishery does not have, so read the absolute value as bracketed between about 18.60 on the farm-gate scale and 34.08 on the full cradle-to-retail scale; the robust part is the ordering, wild above farmed. We rejected the alternative of adding the missing stages onto the meta-analysis figure because it fails its own check: run on farmed prawns it returns 15.03 where Poore & Nemecek gives 26.87, so it would have told you wild prawns are better than farmed when the only like-for-like evidence says they are worse. Basis is edible meat, head-free and shell-free, so weigh peeled prawns rather than the shell-on bag. The rest of the seafood list is on that meta-analysis's narrower farm-gate boundary while this figure is on the fuller Poore & Nemecek one, so small differences between the two sets are not meaningful.

items.calculation_notes: This comes from a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood -- Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', pooling 1,690 fish farms and 1,000 fishery records, published via Our World in Data. The value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across all those studies rather than a plain average of them. Its boundary stops at the farm gate, or at landing for wild capture: processing, transport to retail, retail, packaging, supply-chain losses, and methane and nitrous oxide from aquaculture ponds are all excluded, whereas the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for meat, dairy, plants -- and for the Farmed fish item in this same seafood list -- do include them. Completing this boundary would raise the figure by roughly 20-30%, so every seafood number from this source reads low against the rest of the app. That is why salmon at about 5.1 sits below the farmed-fish item at 13.63 even though both are farmed fish: the two numbers are on different boundaries and from different studies, so that gap is an accounting difference rather than evidence that salmon is cleaner than tilapia or sea bream, and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful. Basis is edible weight -- the muscle fraction -- not as-purchased weight, so weigh the fillet; the source treats 58.5% of live weight as edible, which means a whole round salmon weighs about 1.71x its edible portion. This is the farmed figure, which is what almost all retail salmon is: farmed Atlantic salmon supplies 34 of the source's 39 salmon records, all cage or tank systems rather than ponds, so the pond exclusion does not bite here. Farmed trout is a near-identical 5.41 and shares this item; wild salmon and trout are a separate, higher row at 6.88.

items.calculation_notes: Tuna comes from a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood (Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', via Our World in Data), and the value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across many studies rather than a plain average. The row is the study's tunas, bonitos and billfishes group, 59 fishery records dominated by yellowfin, swordfish, albacore and skipjack; gear matters enormously here, with longline and purse seine differing several-fold per kg landed, and one figure cannot separate them. The boundary stops at landing, so processing, transport to retail, retail, packaging and supply-chain losses are excluded, unlike the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for meat, dairy, plants and the Farmed fish item in this same list -- seafood on this source reads roughly 20-30% low against the rest of the app, and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful. Basis is edible weight, the muscle fraction, not as-purchased weight: weigh the steak or sashimi portion, and note the source treats 61.74% of live weight as edible, so a whole fish weighs appreciably more than its edible part. Tinned tuna logs here on its drained weight, following the US reference amount for canned fish, which is the drained solids; the canning step itself falls outside the source's boundary, so for a tin this is a floor -- read it as 'at least this much'.

items.calculation_notes: Sardines, herring and anchovies come from a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood (Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', via Our World in Data), and the value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across many studies rather than a plain average. The row is the study's small-pelagic group, 176 fishery records all within the herrings, sardines and anchovies family -- Atlantic herring, European sprat, South American pilchard, Atlantic menhaden, European sardine and anchovy, anchoveta and Indian oil sardine -- and the fuel-use literature backs the low figure: purse-seined small pelagics are among the most fuel-efficient fisheries there are. There is no mackerel and no saury in this group, since the study's only two mackerel records sit in its tuna group and saury appears nowhere, so you will find mackerel (saba) and saury (sanma) under this item as the nearest sourced class, but this number is not a measurement of them. The boundary stops at landing -- no processing, transport to retail, retail, packaging or supply-chain losses -- whereas the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for meat, dairy, plants and the Farmed fish item in this same list include all of that, so seafood on this source reads roughly 20-30% low against the rest of the app and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful. Basis is edible weight, the muscle fraction, so weigh fillets rather than whole fish -- the source treats 60.19% of live weight as edible -- and a tin logs on its drained weight.

items.calculation_notes: Mussels, clams and oysters share one row in a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood (Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', via Our World in Data), and the value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across many studies rather than a plain average. It rests on 17 farmed records -- 15 mussel studies and 2 oyster studies, with no clam studies at all, so clams are an extrapolation -- and all 17 are on- and off-bottom systems rather than ponds. The spread behind this number is very wide: wild-harvested bivalves are a separate row at 11.4, more than eight times this 1.4, because of the fuel used by scallop dredging, and Japanese carpet shell (asari) belongs in that wild row rather than this farmed one. The study's own 95% uncertainty range for the farmed figure runs from 0 to 4, and another team puts bivalves at 3-4, so read this as 'lowest in the seafood group' rather than as a precise value; shell-formation CO2 and live transport sit outside the boundary too, as do processing, transport to retail, packaging and supply-chain losses, which the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for meat, dairy, plants and the Farmed fish item in this same list do include -- so this number cannot be set beside those, and small differences across the two sets are not meaningful. Basis is edible weight, and for bivalves the shell is most of what you buy: the source treats only 20.33% of live weight as edible, so shell-on weight is about 4.92x the meat weight and a 1 kg bag in the shell is roughly 203 g of meat. Weigh shucked meat -- every portion size offered here is shucked meat.

items.calculation_notes: Crab and lobster share one row in a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood (Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', via Our World in Data), and the value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across many studies rather than a plain average. Of its 110 fishery records, 82 are lobsters -- mostly red rock lobster and Norway lobster or langoustine -- and 28 are crabs, and the study publishes no separate crab figure: its own fuel-use records put the two halves about 3.3x apart with crab the lower, so this number materially overstates crab and we make no claim about crab specifically. It is the highest figure in this seafood set. The boundary stops at landing, so processing, transport to retail, retail, packaging and supply-chain losses are excluded, while the Poore & Nemecek 2018 figures used for meat, dairy, plants and the Farmed fish item in this same list include them -- seafood on this source reads roughly 20-30% low against the rest of the app, and small differences between the two sets are not meaningful. Basis is edible weight, meaning picked meat: the source treats 30% of live weight as edible, so a whole crab or lobster bought as-purchased weighs about 3.33x its picked meat, and every portion size offered here is picked meat.

items.calculation_notes: Farmed seaweed from a Bayesian meta-analysis of seafood (Gephart et al. 2021, 'Environmental performance of blue foods', via Our World in Data), where the value is the central estimate from a statistical model fitted across many studies rather than a plain average. This one is per kilogram of DRY seaweed at the farm gate, not fresh or rehydrated weight -- the study expresses plants on a dry basis because water loss varies so much after harvest -- so weigh it dry, before soaking. Dry seaweed weighs very little: a sheet of nori is about 3 g and a dried serving about 5 g, so a normal portion is a tiny fraction of a kilogram. The inventory is 20 records spread across Gracilaria, Porphyra (the nori genus), Saccharina, Laminaria and Macrocystis, so it is a mixed farmed-seaweed figure and not a nori figure. Crucially it stops at the farm gate: the washing, sheet forming, drying, roasting and packaging that turn cultivated Porphyra into a sheet of nori are all excluded, and the study itself warns that a large share of seaweed emissions can occur at the drying stage, so read this as a floor rather than the footprint of a packet of nori. Because it is a dry weight on a farm-gate boundary, it cannot be set beside per-kilogram figures for fresh foods, including the Poore & Nemecek-sourced items elsewhere in this app, which run all the way to retail.

items.calculation_notes: Global mean for the row Poore & Nemecek 2018 label 'Wheat & Rye', including land-use change and supply-chain losses. Bread is the product they measured rather than a grain we then applied to bread: their stated unit is 1 kg of bread (variable protein wheat), and because their supply chain ends at the retail shelf, milling and baking are already counted -- the processing stage is about 0.21 of the 1.57, roughly 13% of the total. What is genuinely left out is everything after the shelf: the trip home, toasting, and bread binned at home. 'Variable protein wheat' is their own wording. Weigh bread as bought; the figure is stored as 1.57, so display rounding may show 1.6. Dry pasta carries a higher number than this, but the gap is water, not farming: pasta is worked out from this figure by re-basing it onto pasta's much lower moisture, so it is not evidence that pasta is worse to produce.

items.calculation_notes: Poore & Nemecek 2018 measure oils per litre of refined oil rather than per kilogram, and palm oil appears only in their stage-by-stage breakdown, which totals about 7.32 per litre. Converting that to a weight uses the density implied by the USDA composition record for palm oil -- 1 tablespoon at 13.6 g, or about 0.920 kg per litre -- so about 7.32 divided by about 0.920 gives the 7.96 per kg shown here, roughly 9% above the published per-litre figure. Two caveats are worth knowing. First, the teaspoon and cup portions of that same USDA record both imply a slightly lower 0.913 kg per litre, so the 13.6 g tablespoon is the odd one out; on the other density this would be about 8.01. The figure here is deliberately kept consistent with the 13.6 g spoon preset, so that the number and the preset cannot disagree, and any future revision has to move both together. Second, refined palm oil is semi-solid at room temperature, so a litre of it is not a well-defined quantity: Codex Alimentarius can only quote its density warm, at 50C, while the Japanese (MEXT) table gives an ambient 0.900 kg per litre, which would put this at about 8.13. Read the value as a band of roughly 7.96 to 8.13, about 2% wide -- a caveat on measuring oil by volume, not on the arithmetic. This is a global mean from farm to retail, including land-use change and supply-chain losses, and land-use change alone is about 2.76 of the 7.32 per litre, some 38% of the total. Palm and olive oil are not a fair comparison: the ordering between them reverses on a production-only basis. Weigh the oil as poured.

items.calculation_notes: Per kg of DRAINED canned beans -- unlike the dry-basis Beans / lentils item, this factor is multiplied by the drained weight you eat. Not in Poore & Nemecek; assembled as the mean of two constructions: (a) the CarbonCloud US canned-bean model 1.10 kg CO2e/kg as-sold divided by the USDA Food Buying Guide drained fraction (10.5 oz drained per 15.5 oz can, i.e. 298 g per 439 g = 0.677) = 1.62; and (b) a bottom-up build from the Poore & Nemecek dry-pulse factor (1.79 / 2.5 hydration = 0.72 content) plus the canning and can share of the same model (0.99) = 1.71. Mean 1.665, rounded up to 1.7. Canning energy is small but the steel can is not: packaging is the largest single share of a canned bean's footprint. Tidaker et al. 2021 (0.8 kg CO2e/kg, carton-packed, Sweden) is the peer-reviewed lower bound. Beans cooked from dry are roughly half this per drained kg -- use the Beans / lentils item with dry weight.

items.calculation_notes: Not in Poore & Nemecek, which predates the category; assembled from the two flagship burger LCAs: Beyond Burger 3.4 (Heller & Keoleian 2018, cradle-to-distribution) and Impossible Burger 3.5 (Quantis 2019, cradle-to-gate), mean 3.45. Both are company-commissioned and use boundaries narrower than the rest of this dataset (no retail or supply-chain losses), so a conservative 1.3x uplift is applied: 3.45 x 1.3 = 4.49, rounded up to 4.5. Independently corroborated by Detzel et al. 2021 (ifeu institute, EU-funded): real meat substitutes span 2.4-3.9 kg CO2e/kg cradle-to-gate, and the independent mean (3.26) with the same boundary uplift reproduces ~4.5. The commissioned anchors sit mid-range of the independent values, so the uplift compensates the boundary, not a commissioner bias. A category average spanning simple soy mince to formulated patties; recipes and factory energy genuinely differ. The 113 g patty preset matches the beef patty preset so the burger comparison is like for like.
